Προτιμώ απερίφραστα να είμαι μόνος μου, κρυφακούοντας ηδονοβλεψικά άλλα πε…
items.descriptionOriginal: “Just one?” This is a question I get asked often, and I’m happy to answer with variations of yes. “That’s right. You got it. One indeed!” It has never bothered me, and on the contrary, it fills me with a tiny sense of self-actualized pride. Dinners, movies , concerts. I unequivocally prefer to be on my own, voyeuristically eavesdropping on other people’s lives. To be clear, I like other people’s company in spurts and love, for lack of a better word, “collecting” people as I move through life. But solitude , for the most part, fits best. This is especially true when it comes to traveling. Swiping that train card, with no one watching my clock, fills me with pure glee. But on a recent trip to my favorite city, London, I hit a bit of a snag. High tea at The Kensington, Photo byCecily Knobler Just one? After joyously getting lost in two red-and-gold-swathed parks, I decided it was time for high tea. So I returned to The Kensington Hotel (where I was staying) and made a reservation for that day at 4:00 p.m. “Just you, Ms. Knobler?” the kind man with the top hat asked at the desk. “If that changes,” I said with a wink, “I’ll let you know.” Clad in a black cashmere sweater and a pink and black checkered miniskirt, I checked in with the hosts right on time. They showed me around the various delicate rooms, so that I could pick my spot. Would it be the library, surrounded by leather-bound books by Dickens? Near a fireplace lightly decorated with silver Christmas tinsel? I settled on a seat by a bay window, as the last drops of the sun were squeezed into the space. But I started to notice, as so many families and friends were seated near me, that it seemed this high tea ritual was meant for two or more. And I began to get a little self-conscious. Was I dressed formally enough? Why did it seem I had cat hair on my sweater (and yet don’t have cat?) What exactly IS Christmas pudding? (Luckily, I didn’t have to answer the final question.) Duchess Anna of Bedford For a little context, the late afternoon tea didn’t become popular until the mid-1800s. In a piece about it for Historic UK , Ben Johnson writes, “afternoon tea was introduced in England by Anna, the seventh Duchess of Bedford, in the year 1840. The Duchess would become hungry around four o’clock in the afternoon.” She simply got too hungry to wait for dinner. Johnson continued, “The evening meal in her household was served fashionably late at eight o’clock, thus leaving a long period of time between lunch and dinner. The Duchess asked that a tray of tea, bread and butter (some time earlier, the Earl of Sandwich had had the idea of putting a filling between two slices of bread) and cake be brought to her room during the late afternoon. This became a habit of hers and she began inviting friends to join her.” The last sentence is key. Friends would join her. Johnson further explains, “This pause for tea became a fashionable social event. During the 1880s upper-class and society women would change into long gowns, gloves and hats for their afternoon tea, which was usually served in the drawing room between four and five o’clock.” Christmas tree at The Kensington Hotel, Photo by Cecily Knobler And yet here I was in my version of long gown just being served alone. And as each presentation was given, from the choice of tea to champagne to finger sandwiches, I had this realization that moments are so fleeting. As each item is served and devoured, we must have immediate gratitude because in an instant…it’s gone! Being with just my thoughts (and these exquisite éclairs) sort of forced an introspection I’m not sure I’d have had otherwise. More than enough But gratitude and presence aren’t exactly novel ideas, though they stood out during the ritual. What especially struck me is how powerful it felt to actually enjoy my own company. After all, Duchess Anna had originally begun the tradition as a solo act. Neither she nor I needed a companion to experience every bit of deliciousness life so often has to offer. That high tea with “only” me was more than enough. View this post on Instagram There will, most likely, always be another cucumber sandwich, another date, another teapot. But having the ability to reclaim a ritual and make it my own was truly one of the most special moments of the trip. I’d do it a thousand more times, if I could. (That said, I did chime into a conversation at the table next to me at one point, when I heard them disparaging the Dallas Cowboys.) On my way out, the man in the top hat asked how everything was. “Just right,” I said. “And for the record, it didn’t change. And it was just perfection.” The post High tea is meant to be shared. Doing it alone in London taught me a profound life lesson. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Mr. Feeny, the iconic teacher and principal at the heart of Boy Meets World , was brought to life and made unforgettable by the acting talents of William Daniels. However, it almost didn’t happen. Daniels famously quit the show after the very first table read of the pilot script. He had too much respect for “the underpaid, underappreciated teachers of this country to portray one of them a fool,” per Daniels’ own biography . He didn’t want to play a goofball educator who was only there for laughs. Luckily, the role was rewritten, Daniels returned to the cast , and the rest is history. But of all the heartfelt, emotional, and wise moments Daniels’ brought us as Feeny, one is permanently etched into the hearts of anyone who grew up watching the show. Mr. Feeny’s iconic farewell The series finale of Boy Meets World , “Brave New World: Part 2”, aired in 2000; well over 20 years ago now. But many Millennials can still remember watching the show’s final scene as if it were yesterday. Mr. Feeny gathers in the classroom with his students Cory, Topanga, Shawn, and Eric one final time. As the seventh season of the show comes to a close, each of the main protagonists is preparing to finally leave the nest. They’ll all be moving away from Philadelphia for the first time, finally leaving Feeny behind. He leaves them with parting words of advice: “Believe in yourselves. Dream. Try. Do good.” Topanga, ever the A-plus student, asks if he means “Do well.” “No, I mean ‘do good’,” he responds. Tearful goodbyes ensue, and the kids go on their way out into the big world. Why Mr. Feeny delivered his final words to an empty classroom The series doesn’t end when Topanga, Cory, Shawn, and Eric file out of Feeny’s classroom for the last time. Standing alone once they’re gone, Feeny delivers perhaps his most famous line: “I love you all. Class dismissed.” It’s a full-circle moment for the Feeny character, to finally admit that even though he was hard on the core students, even though he always kept their relationship professional and fair, yes, he did love them in a unique way and not just the way he loves all of his students. Admitting it to an empty room only added to the payoff. And it also allowed the audience to feel like Feeny, the protective mentor we all wish we’d had, was saying goodbye and “I love you,” directly to us. It’s an incredibly moving and poignant end to a show that meant so much to so many. The emotion inside the scene is what makes it so memorable, and much of it was incredibly real. William Daniels recalls being close to tears while filming his final moment. To this day, Feeny is remembered as one of the best portrayals of a teacher ever to grace the screen; and perhaps one of the most beloved sitcom characters of all time. To kids who grew up watching the show, Feeny’s tough love and wisdom was very real. His final line was the catharsis we all needed as the show came to its inevitable end. items.descriptionOriginal: A new Girl Scout cookie , on sale in January, started with a snack that sent a baby to the emergency room . The baby was Denise Woodard’s daughter, Vivienne, and the snack had just two ingredients, peanuts and corn. Vivienne turned out to be allergic to corn, along with eggs, tree nuts and bananas. Woodard, then a sales executive at Coca-Cola, immediately pictured her daughter growing up as the “allergy kid” with the “allergy snacks,” she told Snack Food & Wholesale Bakery magazine. The allergy-friendly options in stores didn’t impress her, so she started baking her own cookies, free of the most common allergens. View this post on Instagram She launched Partake in 2016, selling cookies store by store out of her car, and eventually left Coca-Cola to run it. Keeping it afloat took her 401(k) and then her engagement ring. At least 86 investors turned her down, Woodard told CBS News in 2022. “I took it pretty personal,” she said. View this post on Instagram The first yes came in 2019 from Marcy Venture Partners, the fund Jay-Z co-founded, which led a $1 million round. According to Partake , that made Woodard the first Black woman to publicly raise $1 million for a packaged food startup. That same year, when Partake had exactly one other employee, Woodard told her they were going to make a Girl Scout cookie one day. “I think she thought I had lost the plot!” Woodard told TODAY . Rihanna and H.E.R. later invested, and Partake’s cookies are now sold in thousands of stores. In September, the Girl Scouts announced Girl Scout Sparkables, their first allergy-friendly cookie, developed with Partake. Sparkables are crunchy oatmeal cookies with chocolate chips and colorful sprinkles. They’re vegan and gluten-free, and they’re made in a facility that keeps out the nine major food allergens: peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish and sesame. They go on sale Jan. 12, when Girl Scout Cookie season opens nationally, or sooner in areas where the local season starts earlier. They’re sold only online, for direct shipping, so they won’t turn up at cookie booths. As with other Girl Scout Cookies, the proceeds go to local councils and troops. One of the Girl Scouts selling them will be Vivienne, now in sixth grade. In a Q&A marking Partake’s 10th anniversary this summer, she said, “It makes me happy to know that other kids can feel included like me.” The post Mom started baking Girl Scouts cookies her allergic daughter could eat. Now she’s raised $30 million. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: What's a birthday party without balloons? For Bengaluru-based entrepreneur and mother of two, Sowmya Jagannath, this was a question she found herself thinking about while planning her daughter's birthday. She wanted to try something different, but would her daughter feel that something was missing? Her daughter loves animals, so Sowmya chose colourful fabric decorations in green and earthy shades. Fabric bunting hung across the room, bringing the animal-themed party to life. There were no balloons to inflate or plastic streamers to pull down after the guests left. Instead, the decorations could be packed away and used again at another celebration. The children had fun, and all of Sowmya's initial worries turned out to be unnecessary. Neither her daughter nor the other children missed the balloons. The decorations came from Matter Party, a Bengaluru-based startup that rents out reusable party d cor made from post-consumer textile waste. Founded by Bhavna Kanoria in March 2025, it offers themed fabric decorations that families can rent, return and pass on for another celebration, instead of buying new items that may be discarded after a single use. For Bhavna, the idea began at home, when her own daughter asked for a planet-themed birthday party. The two made buntings from an old sari , finding a way to make the occasion special with fabric they already had. What began with making planet-themed bunting from an old sari for her daughter's birthday eventually inspired Bhavna to start Matter Party in Bengaluru. That small experiment stayed with Bhavna. It would eventually become a business built around a simple question: could celebrations be beautiful, convenient and less wasteful at the same time? How an old sari sparked a business idea Bhavna has a master's degree in English literature, studied interior design and previously worked as a designer. She had also explored ways of making gifting more thoughtful through earlier ventures, including a gift registry service called Giftistree and Scift, a social gifting platform that allowed people to donate to a cause instead of giving physical presents. The idea for Matter Party, however, took time to develop. After making the fabric bunting with her daughter, Bhavna left it on the back burner for a few years. Towards the end of 2024, she returned to it, thinking about how the same principle could work on a larger scale. Matter Party launched in March 2025. Her first rental was for a Lohri celebration rather than a birthday party. The booking came through a friend of a friend, giving her an early opportunity to see how the idea might work beyond her own home. The business now sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala, a Bengaluru-based waste management organisation with a textile recovery facility. Bhavna buys discarded fabric by weight, with material sorted by colour, and sends it to a tailoring unit to be stitched into decorations. "I work on the designs and handle much of the finishing myself, including attaching cords by hand. The leftover scraps are returned to the recovery facility," she says. The result is a collection of reusable decorations in around 35 themes, from unicorns and dinosaurs to Superman, Harry Potter, rainbows and rustic-chic themes. Families can mix and match colours to suit their party. Matter Party sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala and transforms the discarded fabric into colourful party decorations. Lightweight and fitted with cords at both ends, the pieces can be tied to existing fixtures without complicated installation. Once a party is over, the kit is collected and prepared for its next outing. Bhavna irons the fabric, spot-cleans it with soap and water, replaces cords where needed and checks the decorations before they are rented out again. The aim is to keep the materials in use for as long as possible. For these decorations to make their way into more homes, Bhavna knew she had to make renting them as easy as possible for busy parents. What makes parents choose reusable decorations? When Bhavna began offering reusable party d cor, she realised that leading with sustainability did not always persuade people to try it. "People may not choose it just because it is sustainable," she explains. For many parents, the first questions are more practical: Will the decorations look good? Will they suit the theme? Will they be easy to put up? Will renting them be worth the cost? Each decoration is designed to be used across multiple celebrations, allowing families to rent, return and reuse party d cor instead of buying new ones. That understanding has influenced how she presents Matter Party. She wants families to choose the decorations for their designs, range of choices and convenience, without feeling that they have to compromise on how their child's birthday party looks. The reduced pricing is another part of making the service accessible. The startup currently offers two rental options: a Mini Kit for Rs 1,750, which includes 8-10 buntings and fringes, suited to home parties and smaller venues, and a Party Kit for Rs 3,500, with 16-20 buntings and fringes for larger spaces such as clubhouses and gardens. Both kits also include door or backdrop nets, wreaths and a 'Happy Birthday' banner. A refundable security deposit is charged separately. Customers can book through WhatsApp, choose a kit and arrange for delivery before their event. The decorations are collected after the celebration, so families do not have to find storage space for items they may use only once a year. Bhavna has also tried to make the process of putting up and taking down the decorations simple. The kits arrive ready to use, with cords that can be tied to existing fixtures, and customers can pack them back into the provided bag after the party. Optional party helpers are also available through a service partner for families who need additional support. Sowmya found that the rental model made financial sense, too. When she compared the cost with what she had spent buying decorations separately, she realised how quickly individual purchases could add up. "I had done a calculation of the cost of the balloons and the buntings and all the other stuff that I had bought the previous year, and this was actually cheaper than that. We don't realise because we buy it in parts. One balloon package, one streamer package, then this and that. By the time you add it all up, it actually comes up to the same thing, if not more," she says. From dinosaurs and unicorns to rainbows and Harry Potter, Bhavna's reusable fabric decorations are available in around 35 themes for families to choose from. For Bhavna, this is the kind of shift that could help reusable d cor reach more families: it needs to meet their everyday needs as well as help them reduce waste. 'The children don't miss the balloons' Sowmya has used Matter Party for celebrations built around her children's changing interests. Along with her daughter's animal-themed party, her son has had a Harry Potter-inspired celebration in red and black, and the family has also tried a cricket theme. "The themes will be there, but colours are always the easiest thing to put together in terms of adding that vibe to the party. I love that she has so many different colour options," she says. The designs have also drawn attention from other parents. At her daughter's birthday in September, guests could not stop admiring the d cor. Those conversations have given Sowmya a chance to talk about the idea with other families. An earlier conversation with Bhavna about balloons and the impact they can have on animals had encouraged Sowmya to try celebrating without them. "I was almost scared because I was like, 'Oh my God, if I don't have balloons at the party, how will I manage? Will my daughter be okay?'" she recalls. But the children were happy without them. "Nobody missed the balloon completely. Sometimes you have to take these steps to experience yourself; a balloon is not everything for a party," she says. Shwetha, another Bengaluru-based mother of two girls aged 13 and nine, came to Matter Party for a similar mix of thoughtful design and a more sustainable approach. After every celebration, Bhavna irons and spot-cleans the fabric decorations, replaces cords where needed and prepares the kits for their next rental. "I would try and reuse as much as possible, but having said that, options were limited. So I was very pleased that Bhavna came out with a solution which was a little more comprehensive," she says. Shweta has since used the kits for her daughters' birthdays, including garden and rainbow themes. She likes the range of choices and the convenience of having the d cor delivered and collected. A small placard explaining that the decorations are sustainable also gives guests a way to understand the idea. "Keeping sustainability aside, the design is impeccable. She's thought of various options that you would want to host a party. It's definitely something that people should go for even keeping sustainability outside of it," Shweta says. For Bhavna, feedback like this reinforces the importance of making reusable d cor attractive and practical in its own right. Over 100 kg of fabric gets a second life Since its launch, Matter Party has upcycled more than 100 kg of post-consumer textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. For now, the startup operates only in Bengaluru. Bhavna is mindful of the emissions involved in transporting the kits over long distances and does not want expansion to undermine the purpose of the business. She is also exploring collaborations with party venues, caf s, restaurants and other vendors, along with workshops in schools that could help children understand how celebrations can generate less waste. The business has grown through repeat customers and word of mouth, but Bhavna knows that making sustainable choices commonplace will take more than one rental service. It also means helping families see that they do not have to give up the excitement or personal touches that make a birthday special. That change can extend beyond the decorations. Sowmya, for instance, has given plants as return gifts at her daughter's birthday and has chosen plantable pencils and stationery on another occasion. Bengaluru mother Sowmya Jagannath chose Matter Party's reusable fabric decorations for her daughter's animal-themed birthday, celebrating without balloons. Shweta says using the kits has made her think about what else she might change when planning an event. Bhavna has noticed a similar openness among children in her own family. Her niece and nephew, aged three and six, have started telling their friends to avoid waste. For her, it is a reminder that children can adapt to different ways of celebrating, particularly when those choices are part of the experience from the beginning. Helping families celebrate with less waste Bhavna hopes to grow Matter Party without losing sight of what made her start it: the possibility of making a familiar part of family life less wasteful, without making it less joyful. She does not expect parents to change every habit at once. Choosing reusable decorations, skipping balloons or rethinking return gifts can be a starting point. "The aim is to make these options feel normal rather than like an extra effort reserved for particularly environmentally conscious families," she adds. Since launching in March 2025, Matter Party has upcycled over 100 kg of textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. That is also why she wants to expand through local partnerships instead of simply shipping kits across the country. For her, the way the business operates matters as much as the product it offers. A birthday party may last only a few hours, but the decorations can be part of many more celebrations. For Bhavna, that is the possibility she wants more parents to discover: the colourful bunting that made one child's birthday special could bring just as much joy to another child, without either family having to buy everything new. items.descriptionOriginal: When the Delhi house where artist Sumakshi Singh spent her childhood summers was demolished, she found an extraordinary way to bring it back. Using delicate white threads, she recreated its doors, windows, stairs and even its gates. Thousands of kilometres away in Venice, Italy, her childhood home became part of an exhibition that drew around 4.5 lakh visitors. Alongside her work stood a towering bamboo structure inspired by Indian construction sites, a miniature Ladakhi settlement made from discarded egg trays and paper, and sculptures inspired by India's natural landscapes. On 25 November 2026, these creations earned India the Visitors' Lion for Best National Participation at the Venice Biennale, one of the world's biggest international art exhibitions. The award was decided by public vote. The winning exhibition brought together installations made from thread, bamboo, cotton, paper and earth, each telling a different story of India. Photograph: (Instagram/@pibindia) Behind the winning exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home , are five Indian artists who took inspiration from everyday materials, childhood memories and generations-old traditions to explore something we can all relate to: what it means to call a place home. Here are the five artists and the fascinating stories behind their creations. 1. Sumakshi Singh: A house recreated in thread Artwork: Permanent Address Imagine walking into a house that is no longer there. That is the experience Sumakshi Singh creates with Permanent Address , an intricate, life-size reconstruction of her family home in Delhi. The artist has recreated the house using embroidered thread and water-soluble fabric. Artist Sumakshi Singh recreated her childhood home in Delhi using delicate white threads, preserving memories of a house that no longer exists. Photograph: (Instagram/@ abirpothi ) The house was built in 1951 by Singh's grandparents, who came to India during Partition. It became the venue for family weddings, reunions and childhood sleepovers. It was also where she spent afternoons learning to knit and embroider with her grandmother. Years later, when the house was demolished, the same craft helped her recreate the place she had always called home. 2. Asim Waqif: Bamboo that tells a story of changing cities Artwork: Chaal Using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, artist and architect Asim Waqif built a 30-foot-high structure in Venice without using a single nut or bolt. The bamboo pieces are bent and tied together, forming a structure that resembles the scaffolding that supports buildings across Indian cities. Made using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, Asim Waqif's installation highlights traditional building materials and craftsmanship. Photograph: (Instagram/ @indiainvenice ) The choice of material is central to the artwork. Bamboo has long been used in traditional construction, but modern building practices increasingly favour materials such as steel and aluminium. Waqif's installation draws attention to this shift and the risk of losing traditional skills, such as bending and tying bamboo to build scaffolding. 3. Ranjani Shettar: A garden suspended in the air Artwork: Under the Same Sky In contrast to Waqif's towering structure, Ranjani Shettar's installation feels like stepping into a floating garden. Inspired by flowers and natural growth, Under the Same Sky features sculptural forms suspended from the ceiling. Shettar created the flower-like sculptures using handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer. Ranjani Shettar's Under the Same Sky transforms handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer into flower-like sculptures suspended in the air. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Working from her studio near Sagara in Karnataka, Shettar has used these materials for nearly two decades. Her installation allows visitors to experience the garden from within. 4. Skarma Sonam Tashi: Bringing Ladakh's homes to Venice Artwork: Echoes of Home What does a traditional Ladakhi settlement look like when recreated thousands of kilometres away? Artist Skarma Sonam Tashi offers an answer through Echoes of Home , an installation inspired by the architecture and landscape of Ladakh. Using papier-m ch , cardboard, egg trays and old paper, he creates a miniature settlement that evokes the region's traditional homes, built using earth, stone and timber. Inspired by Ladakh's traditional architecture, Skarma Sonam Tashi's Echoes of Home recreates a miniature settlement using discarded egg trays, cardboard, papier-m ch and old paper. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Growing up in Ladakh, Tashi was familiar with traditional homes built using locally available earth, stone and timber. Designed for the region's harsh climate, these houses help keep families warm during winter and cool during summer. As concrete and steel buildings increasingly replace traditional homes, his artwork draws attention to generations of knowledge that Ladakh risks losing. 5. Alwar Balasubramaniam: When nature becomes the artist Artworks: Drift and Not Just for Us Sometimes, the most compelling artwork is made from something as familiar as the ground beneath our feet. For these works, artist Alwar Balasubramaniam, also known as Bala, uses clay and soil sourced from rural Tamil Nadu to create sculptural panels. The surfaces are marked by natural cracks and fissures, capturing the effects of time and environmental forces. Rather than smoothing over these imperfections, the artist makes them the focus of the work. Alwar Balasubramaniam's Drift and Not Just for Us use Tamil Nadu soil to capture nature's marks and patterns. Photograph: ( Indian Pavillion ) While the artwork was being created, peacocks, monkeys and snakes passed through the work in progress, leaving their marks on it. It is a reminder of the idea behind his work: the earth is home to every living creature. Five artists, one idea of home India returned to the Venice Biennale after seven years with an exhibition built around materials familiar to millions of Indians: bamboo, thread, cotton, paper and earth. Through their creations, the five artists brought stories of Partition, traditional architecture, family memories, craftsmanship and India's changing landscapes to an international audience. The exhibition celebrated India's diverse artistic traditions, bringing stories of memory, nature and heritage to a global audience. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) With around 4.5 lakh visitors and an award decided by the public, their exhibition showed how stories rooted in everyday Indian life could resonate with people across the world. Sources: India in Venice 'An Indian postcard from Venice: Why a pavilion at 'Olympics of the art world' matters' by Trisha Mukherjee & Divya A for The Indian Express, Published on 23 September 2026. 'India wins the Visitors' Lion for Best National Participation at the 61st Venice Art Biennale' by Press Information Bureau

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Forest Restoration Training in Africa Gains Ground in Uganda Reading Time: 3 minutes Forest restoration training in Africa has reached 41 conservation practitioners from 16 countries through a new field-based program in Uganda. Forest restoration training in Africa took a significant step forward this year with a new Uganda-based program . The Tropical Biology Association, working with Kabale University, has now equipped 41 conservation practitioners from 16 African countries with hands-on restoration skills. Participants gathered for two 12-day courses held inside Kibale Forest National Park, which organizers described as a living laboratory for restoration science. The program ran as a two-year partnership funded by the UK Government’s Darwin Initiative. Alongside the field courses, Kabale University developed two new master’s-level modules in forest restoration. Those modules are meant to keep producing skilled graduates for government agencies and conservation groups, extending forest restoration training in Africa long after this particular program ends. The Tropical Biology Association has run field-based conservation courses since 1994, with roughly 1,900 alumni working across research, conservation, and policy roles today. Kibale Forest hosts one of Africa’s highest concentrations of primates and has a long history of ecological research through the nearby Makerere University Biological Field Station. That combination of active research infrastructure and degraded forest edges nearby made it a practical setting for hands-on restoration training. Each course combined classroom instruction with fieldwork, covering ecological monitoring, evidence-based restoration planning, and stakeholder engagement. Bringing together participants from so many different countries let people compare approaches and challenges across very different ecosystems. One participant from Nigeria summarized the lesson that stuck with him most: restoration involves far more than simply planting trees. A participant from Tanzania said he learned more in two weeks than in an entire year of prior work, pointing to new monitoring indicators he had never encountered. That feedback reflects a common theme among graduates: technical gaps in monitoring and evaluation, not a lack of enthusiasm, have often limited on-the-ground restoration outcomes. Participants in a forest restoration training in Africa work together on a laptop to analyze field data and strengthen their conservation skills. Photo courtesy of the Tropical Biology Association . Forest restoration projects across Africa have often struggled despite good intentions and available funding. Many efforts have focused heavily on planting while paying insufficient attention to monitoring, community engagement, or long-term maintenance. Forest restoration training in Africa aims to close that gap by building technical skills that keep restoration projects on track long after planting day. One graduate from Kenya’s national forest agency applied a new approach at a degraded river site soon after returning home. Instead of planting across the whole area, she protected existing natural seedlings and planted only in bare patches. That shift cut costs and labor while improving survival rates, and she has since shared the method with dozens of colleagues. Another graduate, based in Ghana, used skills from the course to win a competitive consultancy evaluating community forestry programs nationwide. He has since built those same tools into a large agroforestry project spanning 25 communities and more than a thousand households across Ghana and Kenya. In Ethiopia, a graduate returned to a forest restoration site and helped the local community establish new governance rules for managing it collectively. With an updated monitoring plan, roughly 30 hectares are now under active restoration, with springs recovering and seedling survival rates reaching 80 percent. This push for forest restoration training in Africa connects to a broader continental effort. Programs working under the African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative have pledged to restore more than 100 million hectares of degraded land across the continent. According to the Darwin Initiative, which funds UK government support for biodiversity projects worldwide, building local technical capacity is essential to turning such pledges into results on the ground. Organizers now hope to expand the program to reach 100 restoration managers from more than 20 African countries in the coming years. They also want to help other African universities build similar training into their own degree programs. In other words, forest restoration training in Africa is becoming less about a single course and more about building lasting local capacity across the continent. The post Forest Restoration Training in Africa Gains Ground in Uganda appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Wildlife 2027 Calendars Supporting Conservation Turn Everyday Walls into Year-Round Fundraising Reading Time: 3 minutes From orphaned elephants in Kenya to red fox kits in Virginia, this year’s wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation prove that a simple wall calendar can still fund real protection work. Wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation span continents and causes this year, each turning monthly wall space into sustained fundraising for the species and landscapes they feature. The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s 2027 Calendar brings twelve images from the Orphans’ Project in Kenya, following rescued elephants and other wildlife raised at the trust’s facilities, with every purchase directed toward rescue, protection, and conservation work across the country. The double-page format includes a centrefold poster alongside UK, Kenya, Canada, and USA holidays, pairing each enchanting monthly scene with insight into the orphaned animals’ individual journeys. In South Africa, Crow KZN Wildlife Calendars continue a long-running tradition supporting the Centre for Rehabilitation of Wildlife in KwaZulu-Natal, channeling calendar sales directly into the rescue and rehabilitation of injured, orphaned, and displaced wild animals across the region. These wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation represent some of the most grassroots fundraising efforts on this list, tying purchases to a single rehabilitation center’s daily operating costs. WWF’s 2027 Wildlife Calendars , available through major retail calendar outlets, extend the organization’s global conservation brand into one of its most accessible fundraising products. Featuring iconic endangered species synonymous with WWF’s decades of conservation advocacy, these calendars let supporters bring the organization’s mission into homes and offices while contributing to broader habitat protection and anti-poaching initiatives worldwide. State wildlife agencies produce some of the most enduring entries among wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation. Virginia’s Department of Wildlife Resources marks a milestone with its 2027 edition, celebrating 50 years of the iconic Virginia Wildlife calendar. This anniversary edition features photographs dedicated to juvenile wildlife, refreshed wildlife facts, with a red fox kit by photographer Anne Bryant gracing the cover. Calendar sales support the department’s ongoing wildlife management and conservation programs across the state. The Alaska Wildlife Alliance takes a distinctly participatory approach to wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation. Rather than commissioning professional photography, the organization invites photographers worldwide to submit images through an annual contest, with thirteen winning photographs selected to fill the 2027 Alaska Wildlife Calendar. Winning photographers donate their images and receive complimentary copies in exchange, while all calendar sale proceeds fund the alliance’s work protecting Alaska’s wildlife and wild places. The model doubles as community engagement, turning calendar production itself into a celebration shared between contributing photographers and the conservation mission their images support. Not every wildlife calendar funds a conservation organization directly, but many still advance public appreciation for biodiversity that underpins broader protection efforts. Wildlife photographer Max Waugh’s 2027 collection includes nine themed calendars, five featuring new images and four returning favorites. This year’s new themes include Yellowstone wildlife and scenery, a twelve-species Wild Cats collection photographed in the wild worldwide, a Top Birds collection, a first-ever Borneo calendar highlighting Malaysian wildlife including proboscis monkeys, and a crowdsourced Odd Couples theme capturing interspecies interactions. Returning Classic calendars cover Brazil’s Pantanal and Amazon wildlife, African elephants in black and white, broader animal landscapes, and hornbills and toucans across Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Wildlife photographer Max Waugh’s 2027 Top Birds calendar showcases his favorite wild birds photographed worldwide, one of nine themed calendars he released this year, spanning Yellowstone wildlife, big cats, Borneo species, and more, and advancing public appreciation for biodiversity even without direct conservation funding. Photo courtesy of Max Waugh . What unites wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation across such different organizations and formats is a shared bet that sustained, monthly visual contact with wildlife translates into sustained public support for protecting it. A calendar hanging in a kitchen or office does more than mark dates. Each month’s image becomes a recurring reminder of orphaned elephants recovering in Kenya, native species submitted by state artists, or rehabilitation centers operating on tight budgets in South Africa. This funding model carries genuine significance for smaller organizations in particular. Rehabilitation centers and state wildlife diversity programs often operate without the large donor bases that fund major international conservation groups, making modest, recurring purchases like calendar sales a meaningful and predictable revenue stream. For buyers, the appeal combines practical utility with values-aligned spending, offering a tangible, daily-use product supporting causes they care about without requiring a separate donation decision each time. As 2027 approaches, these calendars demonstrate that even simple products can carry outsized conservation impact when organizations consistently invest in quality photography , compelling storytelling, and transparent connections between purchase and purpose. Whether featuring an orphaned elephant finding its feet in Kenya or a red fox kit marking a state program’s fiftieth anniversary, wildlife 2027 calendars supporting conservation prove that protecting wildlife can start with something as ordinary as checking today’s date. items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking through a forest in the Eastern Himalayas after sunset. The ground is damp, fallen leaves gather beneath towering trees, and the sounds of insects fill the night air. Somewhere among the undergrowth, a tiny frog sits almost unnoticed, blending into its surroundings. In forests like these, some of nature's most fascinating discoveries are easy to miss. And a recent scientific study has brought five such hidden inhabitants into the spotlight. Researchers from the University of Delhi and Harvard University have identified five previously unknown species of horned frogs in Arunachal Pradesh, following five years of fieldwork in the Eastern Himalayas. The discovery has also revealed something unusual about one of them: it feeds on land snails, making it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India. The research offers a fascinating glimpse into the biodiversity that India's forests continue to hold. Meet the five newly discovered frogs All five species belong to the genus Jingophrys , commonly known as diminutive horned frogs. These tiny to medium-sized amphibians are distinguished by horn-like projections of skin around their eyes, which give them their distinctive appearance. The Tanii horned frog (Jingophrys taniitatii) is named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, incorporating the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Photograph: ( The Times of India ) The five newly identified species are: Tanii horned frog ( Jingophrys taniitatii ): Named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, the name also incorporates 'tatii', the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Snail-eating horned frog ( Jingophrys tanogogo ): Named after the Apatani word for snails, this species has an especially unusual diet. Siang horned frog ( Jingophrys siangensis ): Named after the Siang region of Arunachal Pradesh, where it was discovered. Hrdy's horned frog ( Jingophrys hrdy ): Named in recognition of a long-time supporter of herpetological research and conservation biology at Harvard University. Wu-Larson's horned frog ( Jingophrys wularsoni ): Also named to recognise supporters of research and conservation at Harvard. The names of three species acknowledge the region's local communities, language and geography, while the other two honour individuals who have supported scientific research. A frog that eats snails, shells and all! Among the five discoveries, Jingophrys tanogogo stands out for its unusual feeding behaviour. While examining the species, researchers used advanced three-dimensional micro-CT imaging to study its internal anatomy. They found entire land snail shells inside the frog's gut. The snail-eating horned frog (Jingophrys tanogogo) is India's first recorded frog species known to consume land snails, shells and all. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) This makes it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India and the first documented instance of snail-eating behaviour in the family Megophryidae. It is a remarkable finding because it expands what scientists know about the feeding habits of this group of amphibians. Five years of research in challenging terrain Identifying these frogs was no easy task. The research team included Sonali Garg, S D Biju, Tage Tajo, Radhakrishna Upadhyaya K, and James Hanken, who carried out extensive explorations across the Eastern Himalayas. The researchers encountered temperatures as low as minus 4 degrees Celsius while navigating the mountainous terrain. Since these frogs are nocturnal, much of the fieldwork involved searching for them at night, often without a place to stay. Researchers used advanced 3D micro-CT imaging to examine the frogs' anatomy, discovering entire land snail shells inside one species' gut. Photograph: ( The Hindu ) Local tribal communities also played an important role, sharing their knowledge of the region and supporting the researchers during their field explorations. Beyond identifying new species, the team used DNA analysis to understand their evolutionary history. Their findings suggest that the diversification of these frogs coincided with the rise of the Himalayan mountain ranges and the intensification of the Asian monsoon millions of years ago. Why these discoveries matter The findings draw attention to the Eastern Himalayas as an important centre of biodiversity and evolution. The number of Jingophrys species recorded in India has increased seven-fold through this research, while the known diversity of the genus worldwide has more than doubled. Yet, there is still much to learn. Some of these frogs are extremely secretive and appear in remote forests only during short breeding seasons. Further research will be needed to understand their ecology, behaviour and conservation needs. The five-year research involved night-time explorations across the challenging terrain of the Eastern Himalayas, with local tribal communities helping researchers navigate the region. Photograph: ( Indian Expresss ) For now, these five discoveries offer a reminder of how much life remains undocumented in India's forests. Sometimes, finding an entirely new species does not require looking beyond a distant wilderness. It simply requires looking a little closer at the world beneath our feet. Sources: 'New frog species found in Arunachal, Keralam scientist part of team' by K S Sreejith for The New Indian Express, Published on 14 November 2026. 'Two-fold hidden diversity of diminutive horned frogs (Megophryinae: Jingophrys) highlights overlooked in situ diversification in the Himalayas' by PUBMED.

items.titleOriginal: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Turns 100: See This Year’s 9 New Balloons
items.description: Ο Snoopy - ή θα έπρεπε να πούμε ο Joe Cool - θα γιορτάσει κάτι μεγάλο όταν θα επιπλέει στη Νέα Υόρκη κατά τη διάρκεια της παρέλασης της Ημέρας των Ευχαριστιών του Macy 2026. Το alter ego του χαρακτήρα Peanuts είναι μέρος της 100ης απόδοσης της παρέλασης, η οποία αρχικά ήταν προγραμματισμένη να πραγματοποιηθεί σήμερα, αλλά έχει προγραμματιστεί εκ νέου για το πρωί του Σαββάτου λόγω των έντονων καιρικών συνθηκών…
items.descriptionOriginal: Snoopy — or should we say Joe Cool — will be celebrating something big when he floats through New York City during the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. The Peanuts character’s alter ego is part of the 100th rendition of the parade, which was originally slated to take place today but has been rescheduled to Saturday morning due to severe weather. “The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said Wednesday, per NBC News . “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers, and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.” The event began in 1924 and has run annually ever since, except for three years during World War II. Each November, the retail company adds new balloons to its lineup of massive inflatables, a signature feature of the parade almost from the beginning. The first, introduced in 1927, was Felix the Cat, a hit cartoon character from the silent film era . It was designed by Tony Sarg, a puppeteer and illustrator credited with helping turn the parade into the spectacle it is today. George Rinhart—Corbis Historical/Getty Images Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, November 24, 1932. Unlike today, however, the inaugural balloon had to be carried on stilts , as helium wouldn’t be used until the following year. Other aspects also evolved considerably in the ensuing decades, including the long process of bringing a balloon from sketch to showpiece. Artists kick it off with simple drawings, which are then digitally rendered and approved by engineers. Next, a small model is 3D-printed — a physical pattern for the full-scale version that’s made of fabric coated in polyurethane. “[The model] enables us to map out exactly where all of our cuts and all of our seams are going to be,” Will Coss, vice president and head of Macy’s Studios, told Today during a tour of the studio where the balloons are constructed, adding: “Similar to creating a garment for clothing, all of those pieces are the 3D model flattened out.” The final steps are heat-sealing the pieces together, hand-painting the balloon, and adding about 12,000 cubic feet of helium. Just over a century following Felix’s debut, he’s back for this year’s festivities — a decade after his last appearance. He’s joining dozens of other inflatables for a record-breaking 100 in total. Take a look at the nine new balloons created for the centennial celebration. items.title: Οι Portlanders μετατρέπουν το διασωθέν φαγητό σε ποιοτικά γεύματα εστιατορίου
items.titleOriginal: The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals
items.description: Είμαι Τρίτη πρωί στις αρχές Οκτωβρίου και ο σεφ Bradley Cohen, 49 ετών, προσπαθεί να αυτοσχεδιάσει ένα γεύμα από ένα τηγάνι ξενοδοχείου γεμάτο με χοιρινά φιλέτα. Βγάζει ένα κλουβί με φρέσκο ​​λάχανο και κολοκυθάκια από το δωμάτιο, σημειώνοντας την ημερομηνία που έφερε (Κυριακή) και λέει ότι πιθανότατα θα ζεματίσει τα λαχανικά. «Το πρόβλημα δεν είναι ότι δεν υπάρχει αρκετό φαγητό - είναι απλώς μέσα…
items.descriptionOriginal: I t’s a Tuesday morning in early October and chef Bradley Cohen, 49, is trying to improvise a meal from a hotel pan full of pork loins. He pulls a crate of fresh kale and zucchini from the walk-in, noting the date it was brought in (Sunday), and says he’ll probably blanch the veggies. “The problem is not that there’s not enough food — it’s just in the wrong places,” he says. Bradley Cohen is among the chefs who turn donated ingredients into restaurant-worthy meals for Urban Gleaners. Credit: Hannah Wallace He checks out the spices and other ingredients that have appeared in the pantry since his last visit to this centrally located kitchen and grows animated when he finds a container of gochujang, a savory-spicy fermented condiment popular in Korean cooking. “I always get excited when I find this because it adds umami,” he says. He decides on the spot that he’ll make a gochujang-veggie bouillon braising sauce for the pork loins. To complete the meal, he’ll make some macaroni, tossed in butter, garlic powder and paprika. This madcap cooking challenge isn’t for Chopped . It’s for a Portland, Oregon-based gleaning organization. Urban Gleaners is a 20-year-old nonprofit that rescues food before it goes into the waste stream — and helps feed hungry Portlanders. Gleaning, the practice of collecting leftover crops from farmers’ fields or orchards, is nothing new: There are references to gleaning in the Bible, and it was widely employed by the rural poor in the 16th and 17th centuries. And today, there are hundreds of gleaning nonprofits across the U.S. But Urban Gleaners’ cooking program is unique. Helmed by chef Jason Howd, a former pastry chef and caterer who has bee n with the organization for nine years, the cooking program allows part-time chefs like Cohen, a former marketing director, to turn donated ingredients into restaurant-worthy meals. The braised pork, pasta and kale (he ends up sautéing it and tossing in some tomatillo salsa for acid) that Cohen makes today will be refrigerated overnight and packed up the next morning by volunteers, then hand-delivered to shopping-style pantries at local parks, schools and community centers. Perhaps surprisingly, these ingredients aren’t past their sell-by dates. The kale, in particular, looks fresh from the garden. Turns out it was picked two days ago from a nearby farm that sells at the King Farmers Market in Northeast Portland. (Many farms would rather donate surplus fresh organic produce than transport it back to the farm, where they often don’t have storage space.) The pork loins were purchased at a local chef’s supply store. (Donated protein can be hard to come by, so Urban Gleaners has a budget to purchase pork, chicken and other meats.) Delicious prepared meals are just one service Urban Gleaners provides. Haris Kuljančić, the organization’s new executive director, says the need for food has never been greater. The nonprofit delivers about 100,000 pounds of gleaned food per month to roughly 50 locations — including elementary schools, community centers and housing complexes. “We turn it around really quickly,” he says. On this day alone, a Tuesday, the organization will deliver 2,000 pounds of food — mostly gleaned items and prepared food from nearby grocery stores like New Seasons and Zupan’s Market as well as Elephant’s Delicatessen — to a “park market” at Mount Scott Community Center. Urban Gleaners runs three such markets that are open to the public. Urban Gleaners delivers about 100,000 pounds of gleaned food per month to roughly 50 locations. Credit: Hannah Wallace In July 2025, President Trump’s H.R. 1 (aka “the Big Beautiful Bill”) cut SNAP funding — i.e. food stamps — by $186 billion. Tighter eligibility restrictions — such as an 80-hour-a-month work requirement for those under 65 and eliminated benefits for refugees, asylum seekers and houseless folks — have resulted in SNAP participation falling by around 13 percent nationwide , according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities’ SNAP tracker. There are a handful of exemptions (if you’re pregnant, have a child under 14 living with you, or are enrolled in a school or training program, for example) but many SNAP recipients don’t know about these. Another change: H.R. 1 requires that folks reapply for benefits every six months. “They are forcing people to go through the eligibility again, and so if they don’t re-enroll, or don’t jump through all the hoops, you risk losing benefits,” explains Stephanie Barr, executive director of Lift Urban Portland ( Lift UP), a gleaning nonprofit that focuses on feeding neighbors in downtown and Northwest Portland. Needless to say, this can be a challenge for houseless folks (who typically don’t have mailing addresses) and seniors (for whom filling out paperwork can be a burden). In Oregon, these cuts and new restrictions have meant that more than 94,000 Oregonians lost SNAP benefits over the past year, according to the latest data from the Oregon Department of Human Services. This, of course, has led to increased demand at food pantries and the gleaning markets run by Urban Gleaners and others. It’s impossible to fill the void entirely with gleaned food, but Portland area gleaning nonprofits sure are trying. “We hear a lot from the folks we serve about the impacts of SNAP cuts. And the cost of increased food prices,” says Barr, who notes that many of the seniors Lift UP serves are on a fixed income. “Even if you live in affordable housing, your rent can go up. That’s happening in our community.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Lift UP has a shopping-style food pantry in southwest Portland that serves 17,000 people annually. It also delivers food boxes to 550 residents across 50 low-income housing complexes through its “ Adopt a Building ” program. (Lift UP also sponsors pop-up farmers markets in half of those buildings, so residents can access fresh fruits and vegetables.) Like Urban Gleaners, Lift UP mostly gets donations from grocery stores as well as the Oregon Food Bank, community food drives and bakeries such as Grand Central, which makes a “community loaf” especially for anti-hunger organizations. Still, even with all these gleaned groceries, Barr says that over a third of the people that Lift UP serves via Adopt a Building have had to choose between paying rent and buying food. In September, Urban Gleaners threw a Summer Supper fundraiser for their 20th anniversary. Credit: Leesa Morales In 2024, partly in response to cuts to the USDA’s Local Food Purchasing Assistance grants as well as rising grocery costs, Barr and leaders of other Portland-based gleaning and nutrition organizations came together to form a collective called the Coalition to Advance Food Equity (CAFE). “We really need labor, infrastructure and transportation to maximize the gleaned food,” Barr says. The goal of CAFE is to create a more resilient local food system by maximizing bulk purchasing. Eventually the hope is that CAFE will operate a larger physical food hub that all 14 member organizations can use. (Currently, Lift UP’s warehouse works as a de facto food hub. The nonprofit often takes more food than it can use, so the rest is shared with CAFE partners.) So far, CAFE has done a bulk food purchasing pilot project with Costco as well as with local businesses like Bob’s Red Mill. In October, CAFE also launched a “Farm to Food Assistance” pilot with two local regenerative farms, moving 1,000 pounds of organic produce from Stoneboat Farm and CAMPO (Colaboración Agrícola Mobilizando Poder Orgánico) to partner pantries. This is a mutually beneficial investment: Local farms get much-needed income, and the communities that CAFE members feed get high-quality produce. At Urban Gleaners’ summer fundraiser, there were goats on hand so that diners could hand-feed them corn cobs and leftovers. Credit: Leesa Morales Another CAFE member is the Portland Fruit Tree Project (PFTP), a 20-year-old organization that dispatches volunteers around town to pick fruit from Portlanders’ yards — apples, figs, Asian pears, grapes and more. The harvest is then distributed to food pantries, homeless service organizations and other nonprofits. For its Summer Supper fundraiser, Urban Gleaners asked 15 Portland-area chefs to create dishes from mostly gleaned items. Credit: Leesa Morales Excess fruit gets made into jam, syrup or other products to extend its shelf life. Food preserver is the most popular volunteer position at PFTP. “These volunteers come in and look at what we’ve got, and we kind of decide: Are we going to can it? Are we going to dehydrate it? Are we going to juice it and use it later? Are we just going to prep it for the freezer because we’ve got too much to do right now?” says Executive Director Heather Keisler Fornes. “Yesterday we were making plum syrup that’s delicious and it’s bright pink — so pretty.” Kousa dogwood refrigerator jelly and sea buckthorn jelly were two of the more unusual items volunteers recently made. Some of these are sold at farmers’ markets and craft fairs — which helps spread the word about the Portland Fruit Tree Project. Being part of CAFE has many benefits, says Keisler Fornes. “There are times where one group has too much of something, and it’s so easy to be able to then communicate with the entire group and say, ‘Who wants this?’ Then it’s not a burden to anybody,” she says. The different CAFE members even share staff. Busy season for PFTP is summer and fall. After that, some of Keisler Fornes’s staff work for Lift UP or other nonprofits in the CAFE coalition. I n September, Urban Gleaners threw a Summer Supper fundraiser for their 20th anniversary. They asked 15 Portland-area chefs to accede to a unique challenge: Create a dish out of mostly gleaned items. The inventiveness and talent on display was remarkable. Mika Paredes, chef at French-inspired bistro L’Echelle, made a ratatouille tartine with basil and whipped brie. Ryan Roadhouse, who had just won a James Beard Award for his Japanese omakase menus at Nodoguro, created curried Oregon bay shrimp with cherry tomatoes and spiced seaweed. And Jacob Smutko, one of the chefs at Javelina, a unique restaurant focused on the foods of the Indigenous tribes of the Pacific Northwest, made sumac and corn ribs with sikil pak (a traditional Mayan pepita dip made with cherry tomatoes, poblano peppers, onions, lime and cilantro). Emphasizing Urban Gleaners’ mission to fight food waste, there were goats on hand so that diners could hand-feed them corn cobs and leftovers. It was a uniquely Portland experience — celebrating the city’s vibrant food scene while also highlighting the power of upcycled ingredients and supporting an organization that fights food waste and food insecurity at the same time. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime “No one should have to worry where their next meal is coming from, especially when there’s so much perfectly good food available,” says Gregory Gourdet, chef at Haitian restaurant Kann and an Urban Gleaners board member. “I love that Urban Gleaners puts feeding people at the center of its mission while also addressing food waste. It’s not just about rescuing food; it’s about feeding our neighbors, supporting families, and making sure people in our community don’t go hungry.” The post The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.description: Περισσότερα από 400 χρόνια αφότου οι άποικοι πήραν καλαμπόκι, ενόχλησαν τάφους και αντάλλαξαν πυρά με πολεμιστές Nauset κοντά στο Cape Cod της Μασαχουσέτης, 126 στρέμματα αλυκής και προγονικού βιότοπου επιστράφηκαν στην ιθαγενή διαχείριση -- γη που βλέπει στην παραλία όπου έγινε η πρώτη εχθρική συνάντηση. Η Προστασία της Φύσης μετέφερε τ…
items.descriptionOriginal: More than 400 years after colonists took corn, disturbed graves, and exchanged gunfire with Nauset warriors near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, 126 acres of salt marsh and ancestral habitat have been returned to Indigenous stewardship -- land that overlooks the very beach where that first hostile encounter took place. The Nature Conservancy transferred the property to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit founded by Ramona Peters of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, who sees the moment as an opening rather than a closing: "This place holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed." The land has been joined to an adjacent parcel now named T8nup hs Uwatuhsh t -- "at the turtle's nest" in the W pan ak language -- where tribal families are invited to forage, fish, hold ceremony, and belong again to a place their ancestors tended for more than 12,000 years. What the transfer quietly insists upon is that history is not only something to be corrected in textbooks; sometimes it can be corrected in deeds. "Returning this land to Indigenous ownership is historical and an act of resilience after four centuries of dispossession," Peters said -- and in that resilience, something older than the wound is still alive.

items.titleOriginal: Tukaram Omble: The 26/11 Hero Whose Sacrifice Helped Bring Justice
items.description: Ήταν ο πατέρας που έπαιζε καρόμ με τις κόρες του, άκουγε τις ιστορίες τους στο κολέγιο και ποτέ δεν έφερε το άγχος της δουλειάς στο σπίτι. Αλλά στις 27 Νοεμβρίου 2008, ο Tukaram Omble δεν επέστρεψε ποτέ στο σπίτι. Πρώην στρατιώτης του Ινδικού Στρατού και Βοηθός Υπο-Επιθεωρητή στην Αστυνομία της Βομβάης, ο Όμπλ ήταν σε υπηρεσία κατά τη διάρκεια των τραγικών γεγονότων της 26/11 στη Βομβάη. Εμφάνιση extrao…
items.descriptionOriginal: He was the father who played carrom with his daughters, listened to their college stories and never brought the stress of work home. But on 27 November 2008, Tukaram Omble never returned home. A former Indian Army soldier and Assistant Sub-Inspector with Mumbai Police, Omble was on duty during the tragic events of 26/11 in Mumbai. Displaying extraordinary courage and selflessness, the 54-year-old put his duty above his own life. His bravery played a crucial role in helping Mumbai Police bring a key accused into custody. For his exceptional service and supreme sacrifice, Omble was posthumously awarded the Ashoka Chakra. But for his four daughters, he was much more than a decorated officer. He was their closest companion, their go-to person and the father who always reassured them that everything would be alright. That night, he told his daughter Vaishali not to worry about him. He had always kept his work worries away from home. Even in his final hours, he was trying to protect his family from them. India remembers his courage. His daughters remember the man who made home feel safe. #TukaramOmble #2611MumbaiAttacks #MumbaiPolice #AshokaChakra [Tukaram Omble, Tukaram Omble story, 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks, 26/11 heroes, Mumbai Police heroes, Ashoka Chakra awardee]

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News EU Greenwashing Ban for Businesses Puts Proof Behind Green Claims Reading Time: 3 minutes The EU greenwashing ban for businesses is now in effect, giving shoppers clearer and more trustworthy environmental information. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses began applying on September 27, 2026. The European Union (EU) adopted it through the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive . Shoppers now get clearer and more honest environmental information. Greenwashing means making a product sound more eco-friendly than it really is. Under the new rules, vague claims must be backed up with evidence. Terms like “green,” “sustainable,” and “energy efficient” now require excellent environmental performance. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses also targets carbon offset claims. Offsetting means funding projects elsewhere to balance out a company’s emissions. Claims of a neutral, reduced, or positive impact, such as carbon neutral or net zero, cannot rely on offsets. Broad claims face limits too. A company cannot describe an entire product as eco-friendly when only one part is. The same goes for claims about a whole business when only one division qualifies. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses also stops companies from presenting legal minimums as special features. If the law requires recycled content in plastic packaging, brands cannot advertise it as a bonus. Honest marketing now means highlighting what goes beyond the rules. Misleading claims about product lifespan are also off limits. Companies cannot overstate how long a product lasts or claim it allows repairs when it doesn’t. They also cannot nudge shoppers to replace parts or refill consumables earlier than necessary. Sustainability labels face a new test. These rules apply to trust marks like Fairtrade, B Corp, and the Forest Stewardship Council. Labels must come from a public authority or a certification scheme that meets EU standards. An independent third party must verify that each scheme follows its standards. Businesses that display a label stay legally responsible for using only compliant ones. Labels that fail the test can no longer appear in the EU. Promises about the future need evidence. A company that says it will become carbon neutral needs a detailed plan with measurable, time-bound targets. An independent expert must review that plan regularly and share the findings with consumers. Sellers must also give buyers new information before a sale. Physical goods need a reminder about the two-year legal guarantee, using an EU template. Sellers must share details on repairs, spare parts, and software updates when available. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses requires companies promising future carbon neutrality to publish a detailed plan with measurable, time-bound targets reviewed regularly by an independent expert, while sellers must also give buyers information on the two-year legal guarantee, repairs, spare parts, and software updates. Photo by Sarah Chai on Pexels. Smartphones and tablets also need a repairability score. Online sellers must list environmentally friendly delivery options. National regulators in each EU country will enforce the EU greenwashing ban for businesses. Fines can reach 4% of yearly sales in that country, or more under national law. Claimants can also bring class-action-style cases under the Representative Actions Directive. Consider the scale of the 4% cap. A company with €50 million in sales in one country could face a €2 million fine. Accurate claims cost far less. The good news is that the EU greenwashing ban for businesses offers a clear path to compliance. Businesses can audit their websites, packaging, and ads for vague terms. Then they can swap broad slogans for specific, provable facts. Consider a hypothetical clothing brand. Instead of calling its jackets sustainable, it can name the exact share of recycled fabric. A verified label can then support that number. Each EU country writes its own national version of the rules, so details can vary. Germany, for example, limits its future claims rules to consumer sales. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses applies to any trader selling to EU customers, including online sellers. Businesses outside Europe that ship to EU customers should review their claims too. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses gives shoppers practical tools for choosing well. They can compare products using facts instead of vague slogans. They also learn more about repairs, spare parts, and warranties before buying. Companies can read the directive’s official text to see every requirement in detail. Reviewing it helps teams plan website updates and label changes. See also: Blockchain for a Greener Supply Chain: Transparency That Reduces Waste Readers who want to shop with confidence can also learn to spot greenwashing and greenhushing, when a company shares too little about real green efforts. Knowing both helps people judge vague environmental claims. The EU greenwashing ban for businesses rewards companies that do the real work. Shoppers gain a fairer way to judge what helps the planet. The post EU Greenwashing Ban for Businesses Puts Proof Behind Green Claims appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Κάποτε σπάνιο στο Ujani, 10 Lakh Deccan Mahseer Πάρτε μια νέα ευκαιρία μέσω ενός 10ετούς προγράμματος
items.titleOriginal: Once Rare in Ujani, 10 Lakh Deccan Mahseer Get a Fresh Chance Through a 10-Year Plan
items.description: Ένα ψάρι που είχε σχεδόν εξαφανιστεί από τη δεξαμενή Ujani της Μαχαράστρα πριν από δεκαετίες, έχει άλλη μια ευκαιρία να κολυμπήσει στα νερά της. Το Deccan Mahseer, που κάποτε βρισκόταν σε αφθονία στη λεκάνη του ποταμού Bhima, είχε γίνει ολοένα και πιο σπάνιο μέχρι τη δεκαετία του 1990, καθώς η ρύπανση, τα χωροκατακτητικά είδη ψαριών και οι καταστροφικές αλιευτικές πρακτικές επηρέασαν τους ιθαγενείς της δεξαμενής.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A fish that had nearly disappeared from Maharashtra's Ujani Reservoir decades ago is getting another chance to swim in its waters. The Deccan Mahseer, once found in abundance in the Bhima River basin, had become increasingly rare by the 1990s as pollution, invasive fish species and destructive fishing practices took a toll on the reservoir's native aquatic life. Now, in October 2026, the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), with support from the Cipla Foundation and Tata Power, released 45 lakh (4.5 million) native fish fingerlings, including 10 lakh Deccan Mahseer (Tor khudree), popularly known as the 'Tiger of the River', alongside more than 21,000 aquatic plants into Maharashtra's Ujani wetland near Bhigwan. According to BNHS, the restoration programme responds to decades of ecological degradation in Ujani, where invasive fish, deteriorating water quality and destructive fishing practices have contributed to the decline of native species. Why did the fish disappear? Ujani Reservoir, formed by the Ujani Dam on the Bhima River, is an important freshwater ecosystem spanning parts of Pune, Solapur and Ahilyanagar districts. Over the years, however, its aquatic biodiversity has come under pressure from invasive fish, pollution and fishing methods that capture even young fish before they can reproduce. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. Photograph: (Rajeev Raghavan) Invasive species such as suckermouth catfish, tilapia and African catfish have spread through its waters. The BNHS-led restoration programme has also identified the impact of invasive aquatic vegetation , which can obstruct waterways, affect oxygen levels and compete with native plants. The scale of the intervention reflects the extent of the problem. BNHS and local fisheries societies have removed more than 178 tonnes of invasive fish from the reservoir over the past year. Additionally, nearly 6,500 tonnes of invasive vegetation, including water hyacinth, Ipomoea and Prosopis, have been cleared from approximately 2,000 hectares of the catchment area. The October stocking programme included 10 lakh Indian major carps, comprising rohu, catla and mrigal, alongside more than 22 lakh fingerlings of other native species, including kavdas, nukta and bobari. What makes the Deccan Mahseer important? The Deccan Mahseer, also known as the blue-fin mahseer, is a freshwater fish belonging to the carp family. Its historic distribution includes the Krishna River system and its tributaries across parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana. A 2019 scientific review, titled Mahseer (Tor spp.) Fishes of the World: Status, Challenges and Opportunities for Conservation , published in the journal Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries, examined the distribution, conservation status and threats facing mahseer species. This is the Deccan Mahseer, revered as Lord Vithoba's beloved "Devmaasa". Found in Indrayani river, it is now endangered due to pollution deadly water hyacinth growth on Anand Doha. A case of authorities' indifference😢 ##goodbadugly #saverivers Image: iNaturalist (1/2) https://t.co/5aTWC0UhK4 — Pune River Revival (@PuneRivers) May 22, 2024 The researchers identified the northern and central Western Ghats, particularly the Krishna River system, as the historical range of the Deccan Mahseer. Its tributaries include the Indrayani, Mula-Mutha, Koyna, Tungabhadra and Panchaganga. The review also highlighted how artificial propagation and large-scale fish stocking since the 1970s expanded the species' distribution beyond its original range. Some introduced populations have even shown invasive characteristics, affecting native fish populations in other river systems. Another study, published in Fisheries Research in 2011, examined the sustainability of Deccan Mahseer fisheries in the Western Ghats using catch data collected with the participation of local fishers. Researchers Rajeev Raghavan, Anvar Ali, Neelesh Dahanukar and Alison Rosser studied six fishing sites and found that catches frequently included immature fish. Their assessment also indicated that exploitation rates exceeded sustainable levels at most of the sites studied. A 10-year plan to bring the fish back The Ujani restoration programme included a dedicated partnership between BNHS and Tata Power for the conservation of the Deccan Mahseer. Under the arrangement, Tata Power has committed to supplying 10 lakh mahseer fingerlings over 10 years. The fish are being bred with support from its facility at Valvan in Lonavala. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BNHS 💚 Wildlife Conservation (@bombaynaturalhistorysociety) According to BNHS's October 2026 conservation newsletter, Dr Unmesh Katwate, head of the BNHS Wetland Eco-Restoration Project, visited the facility on 9 October to assess the available fingerling stock and preparations for their release. The newsletter also records a separate initial release of 8,000 fingerlings near Palasnath Temple in Ujani Reservoir on 22 October. The site was selected after considering its depth, water quality and habitat conditions. The organisation is also working with local fisheries societies and government departments to encourage more sustainable fishing practices. For Ujani, the return of the Deccan Mahseer is therefore part of a larger restoration exercise. Whether the mahseer can establish a self-sustaining population in the reservoir will become clearer through continued monitoring in the coming years. Sources: 'Tata Power Supports Deccan Mahseerconservation Through Long-Term Commitment' : By Bombay Natural History Society Newsletter, Published On October 2026 'BNHS releases 4.5 million native fish, 21,000 aquatic plants at Ujani Wetland to revive biodiversity' : By Mrityunjay Bose, Published on 19 October 2026

items.title: Συνδύασε το Rajasthani Folk με το Beatboxing!
items.titleOriginal: He Mixed Rajasthani Folk With Beatboxing!
items.description: Γνωρίστε τον Divyansh Kacholia του Jaipur, γνωστό και ως DVK The Beatboxer. Μεγάλωσε ακούγοντας Ghoomar και άλλα λαϊκά τραγούδια του Rajasthani. Στα 13, ανακάλυψε το beatboxing και τελικά βρήκε έναν τρόπο να τους φέρει κοντά. Άρχισε μάλιστα να προπονείται για 9-10 ώρες την ημέρα αφού γνώρισε τον πρωταθλητή του beatboxing Skiller.
