items.descriptionOriginal: Meet Jaipur’s Divyansh Kacholia, aka DVK The Beatboxer. He grew up listening to Ghoomar and other Rajasthani folk songs. At 13, he discovered beatboxing and eventually found a way to bring the two together. He even began practising for 9–10 hours a day after meeting beatboxing champion Skiller. His unique sound took him to the finals of Dil Hai Hindustani in 2018. Later, when his teammates couldn’t make it to the India’s Got Talent audition, he teamed up with flautist Manuraj Singh Rajput. The duo went on to win Season 9! In 2023, they took their act to America’s Got Talent: All-Stars, earning a standing ovation. Judge Heidi Klum summed it up as “Bollywood meets Brooklyn”. From folk tunes heard at home to a global stage, Divyansh has stayed true to his sound. Which of their performances would you watch on repeat? Tell us below! 👇 #DivyanshKacholia #DVK #Beatboxing #FolkBeatboxer #AmericasGotTalent #IndiasGotTalent #Rajasthan #IndianTalent #MadeInIndia [America’s Got Talent: All-Stars, Indian Beatboxer]

items.title: Από το πλύσιμο των πιάτων στο τραγούδι για εκατομμύρια: Ο Talwiinder λέει ειλικρινής για το πώς δίδαξε τον εαυτό του μουσική
items.titleOriginal: From Washing Dishes to Singing for Millions: Talwiinder Gets Candid About How He Taught Himself Music
items.description: Τι κάνεις όταν θέλεις να γίνεις μουσικός, αλλά το δοκιμαστήριο σου είναι ένα φαστ φουντ και ο χρόνος εξάσκησής σου ξεκινά αφού φύγει ο τελευταίος πελάτης; Για περισσότερα από τέσσερα χρόνια, η απάντηση του Talwiinder ήταν να τραγουδάει πλένοντας πιάτα και κλείνοντας το Subway. Άρχισε να εργάζεται εκεί στην Τάξη 10, προσαρμόζοντας το riyaaz (μουσική πρακτική) γύρω από την παραγγελία του πελάτη…
items.descriptionOriginal: What do you do when you want to become a musician, but your rehearsal room is a fast-food outlet and your practice time begins after the last customer has left? For more than four years, Talwiinder's answer was to sing while washing dishes and closing Subway. He started working there in Class 10, fitting riyaaz (music practice) around customer orders and closing duties. Without formal music training, he used the time after serving customers to practise his singing. Today, his music has travelled far beyond that counter. 'Pal Pal', made with Afusic and Ali Soomro, caught the attention of British DJ and producer Fred again.., who played the track during a livestream. Talwiinder saw it just like everyone else watching. It was, he says, "a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene". Between those closing shifts and the livestream were years of teaching himself music, writing songs and continuing to create despite rejection from music labels. From serving customers to writing songs Talwiinder has been singing since he was three or four, but he says the decision to build a life around music came when he began writing songs of his own. Singing was something he loved; songwriting gave that love somewhere to go . The 'Pal Pal' livestream moment connected a Punjabi collaboration with audiences beyond its listening community. Photograph: ( Instagram/@talwiinder ) "The moment I started to write my own songs, I knew I had to release these tracks for people who need it more than me," he tells The Better India . "Once I got into songwriting, I knew this is what I want to do for the rest of my life." There was no ready-made route into the industry. He spent more than four years at Subway, starting in Class 10, and remembers the job fondly for what it taught him about people. "It taught me communication, reading people's energy and having one-on-one conversations with customers to the point where I knew their whole order the moment they stepped in the store," he says. He learnt to run the store by himself. When the rush was over, he had time alone with his thoughts. "That alone time was often used to do riyaaz while cleaning dishes and closing the store," he says. "I loved every bit of that job and never felt like I wanted to quit." His music moves between Punjabi and international listening spaces, opening possibilities for cross-cultural collaboration. Interestingly, someone who once spent hours interacting with customers now prefers to keep conversations brief. He says he prefers texting to phone calls and often avoids conversations because talking for too long tires his throat and voice. He likes to "talk with eyes" and use very few words. He even has a WhatsApp display picture that reads, "Don't call me, text me." Through the songs he writes, however, Talwiinder communicates with millions of listeners. Learning how to express himself through music has involved years of listening to and understanding his own voice. How he taught himself music Without formal music training, Talwiinder learnt by making songs and returning to them. He advises beginners with a laptop or computer to invest in a home-recording setup, which he estimates can cost around $150 to $200, rather than waiting for a professional studio or teacher. "Record yourself as much as you can," he says. "You will understand your voice better. When the time comes and you're in a proper studio with top-notch equipment, you won't be so lost, but excited to go full beast mode." For listeners discovering Punjabi music abroad, Talwiinder offers an entry point into Punjabi sounds. Listening to these recordings helps a singer recognise what needs work and gradually develop a sound of their own. It is something aspiring musicians can begin doing with basic equipment at home. Over time, Talwiinder has also learnt when to stop working on a song and let listeners hear it. He does not believe there is a magical point at which a track becomes perfect. "The song is never ready; there will always be something that can be added or taken out," he says. "You have to trust your gut and give your 100% in stitching the song together, and once it's out, make peace with it and move on to the next song." With every release comes a public tally of streams, views and likes, but Talwiinder says he has never made numbers the measure of his work. He recalls gaining more than four million Instagram followers in a month without paid promotions. He says he has never bought fake views or likes, or followed trends. His focus, he says, is on doing justice to the music, while listeners decide whether to return to it. When he does not feel like starting something new, he returns to his unfinished tracks. "I have way too many unfinished songs," he says. He chooses his favourites and starts finishing them, turning a creative block into a chance to reopen old work. When music labels turned him down The years were not without rejection. Talwiinder remembers approaching labels that did not want to associate with his music. Among the tracks he mentions is 'Khayaal'. The singer's visual aesthetic draws from alternative music culture rather than conventional Punjabi entertainment imagery. "They told me indirectly and did not want to associate with my music," he says. "Funny thing is I still see those labels coming back and asking to work together." He kept making music, including songs that did not immediately find their moment. 'Haseen' was written and recorded in 2019 but released six years later. He says he would not change his older music simply because he has grown as an artist. "I believe good music does not have an expiration date," he says. A song does not lose its value, in his view, because it has been waiting in a folder. With 'Pal Pal', Talwiinder experienced what it was like for his music to reach someone he had not expected. The collaboration with Afusic and Ali Soomro caught the attention of Fred again.. When the British DJ played the track during a livestream, Talwiinder did not hear about it through a label or a carefully arranged announcement. He saw it on the stream, like everybody else. "It caught me by surprise," he says. "It was a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene." With his signature face paint and unconventional styling, Talwiinder has carved out a recognisable space in contemporary music. Having experienced rejection himself, Talwiinder now wants to help other aspiring musicians find people they can work with. Asked what he would do if a young artist arrived with little money and no industry connections, Talwiinder says he would first listen. If the work felt genuine and original, he would connect the artist with his community and suggest collaborators, giving them somewhere to belong. For someone who spent years practising after work and learning to make music on his own, being able to offer another young artist a place to begin is something he now looks forward to.

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν μυστηριώδεις λίμνες περισσότερο από ένα μίλι κάτω από την Ερυθρά Θάλασσα
items.titleOriginal: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
items.description: Περισσότερο από ένα μίλι κάτω από την επιφάνεια της Ερυθράς Θάλασσας, οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν σπάνιες υποβρύχιες λίμνες που θα μπορούσαν να αποκαλύψουν μυστικά για τους αρχαίους ωκεανούς της Γης και την πιθανότητα εξωγήινης ζωής. Γνωστά ως πισίνες άλμης, αυτά τα εξαιρετικά αλμυρά περιβάλλοντα χωρίς οξυγόνο γεμίζουν εκπληκτικά με μικροβιακή ζωή, αμφισβητώντας την κατανόησή μας για το πού ζει…
items.descriptionOriginal: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

items.title: Πώς να είστε ευγνώμονες σε κάποιον - ακόμα κι όταν πραγματικά δεν το θέλετε
items.titleOriginal: How to Be Grateful to Someone — Even When You Really Don’t Want to
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Mark Schroeder , καθηγητή φιλοσοφίας στο USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons . Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Υπάρχουν λίγα μεγαλύτερα συναισθήματα t…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Mark Schroeder , a professor of philosophy at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts, and Sciences, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . There are few greater feelings than the sense of heartfelt gratitude to another human being who has done you a solid. Sincere thanks and reciprocation are part of the glue that binds us in human relationships. But sometimes you’re just not feeling it. You know that you have benefited from what someone has done for you, but you don’t really feel grateful to them for doing it. Most teenagers go through this period with their parents. Maybe you take your partner or colleague for granted. For me, 14 years ago, it was my mother-in-law. She had upended her life to move from South Dakota to California to live with my wife and me to assist with childcare after our daughter was born; no other source of childcare fit with our demanding work schedules and my commute. She made a huge sacrifice that transformed our lives, but there were moments when I really struggled to feel grateful. Since that time, I’ve come to devote much of my research as a philosopher to studying how the way that we interpret each other as people shapes our relationships . That work has helped me to understand why I struggled to be grateful — and taught me a little bit about how to do better. Personal Gratitude I’ve found that the hardest part of feeling grateful to someone is the “to” part. It is one thing to be impersonally grateful that something happened and another thing to be personally grateful to someone for doing it. These are not the same. Both forms of gratitude require seeing something as a benefit. And they both require a humble recognition of how easily things could have been otherwise. When the rain ends a drought, an atheist can feel grateful that the tomatoes will survive. But the atheist isn’t grateful “to” anyone for the rain. AP Photo/Mahesh Kumar A Priests offer prayers to Varuna, the Hindu god of rain, as they stand in the Osman Sagar on the outskirts of Hyderabad, India, on July 16, 2013. Personal gratitude requires more than impersonal gratitude. It is an example of what the philosopher Peter Strawson calls a “participant” attitude : an attitude that we have toward people, but not toward things. And a large theme in my work is that participant attitudes such as gratitude involve giving someone credit for what the attitude responds to. But which benefits we give people credit for is complicated. As philosophers such as Tony Manela have argued, actions motivated primarily by money, self-interest, or insecurity don’t merit personal gratitude , even when they benefit you. Actions motivated by love, generosity, or concern, on the other hand — or other “pro-social” motives — do. Sometimes people fail to feel gratitude because they take someone for granted, not noticing how easily they could have done otherwise. This wasn’t my problem with my mother-in-law. It was obvious that she didn’t have to move across the country to live with us. But it was hard to avoid noticing that she had always wanted to live in California. Sometimes it is hard to feel grateful because of how we interpret someone’s motives. They could have done otherwise, but we don’t think their action was really “about us.” Bad Motives Are Easy to Find Sometimes ungenerous motives can help people to be generous. Your child’s kindergarten teacher isn’t a volunteer. They may be a naturally generous person — but still, they probably wouldn’t be working with your child on spelling, arithmetic, and handling adversity if they weren’t getting a paycheck. It’s still appropriate to be grateful to them. Their financial incentive to show up for work enables their generosity, rather than competing with it. svetikd—E+/Getty Images Your child’s teacher might be generous, but their job enables them to act on that generosity every day. Elementary school teachers are not alone. After all, people’s decisions are often driven by many factors: some that merit gratitude and others that don’t. So if you go looking for selfish motives, you are bound to find some . Take your partner, for example. They do something that benefits you: buying you flowers, filling your tank with gas, or finally taking their turn to wash the dishes. They are partly motivated by generosity, love, or communal spirit. But, as in any close relationship, sometimes they may be hoping to get something out of it : reciprocation, maybe, or getting you off their back. It matters which of these you interpret as their “true” motive: Seeing it one way opens you up to gratitude, while the other precludes it. What Are “True” Motives? The distinction between someone’s “true” motive and the other motives that enable it looks like the distinction between causes and enabling conditions . For example, when you drop a wine glass, the fragility of the glass enables the drop to cause the break, but it isn’t itself a cause of the break — the drop is. In the case of the falling glass, there’s a clear, objective answer to what caused the break and what merely enabled it. But I believe that relating to people is deeply different than understanding physical things. The key question in whether to be grateful to someone isn’t about which motives count as “causes.” It is about which cause we need to bring into focus in order to see the other person more clearly for who they are . See It Their Way In other words, it’s at least partly a matter of perspective. If someone does you a favor, but you know they’re hoping for something in return, you can see that as their “true” motive. But you don’t have to see it that way. Instead, you could see that motive as the condition they need for their generosity to thrive. Shifting perspectives isn’t easy. When you’re doubting someone’s motives , their lack of generosity can feel obvious. But it helps to remember that people tend to believe they’re acting generously . If you want to respond with gratitude, try seeing them as they see themselves. What if that doesn’t work? Well, the next best thing to being grateful to someone is being grateful for them. Starting there is a good way to remind yourself of why you value this relationship in the first place. And it can be enough to simply say “thanks” and mean it. items.title: Η μεγαλύτερη δοκιμή ρομποτικής αντικατάστασης γόνατος στον κόσμο αποκαλύπτει εκπληκτικά αποτελέσματα
items.titleOriginal: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
items.description: Η χειρουργική επέμβαση αντικατάστασης γόνατος με τη βοήθεια ρομπότ προσφέρει μεγαλύτερη χειρουργική ακρίβεια, αλλά μια κλινική δοκιμή ορόσημο αποκάλυψε έναν εκπληκτικό περιορισμό. Παρά την προηγμένη τεχνολογία, οι ασθενείς δεν εμφάνισαν σημαντικές βελτιώσεις στον πόνο, την κινητικότητα ή την ανάρρωση σε σύγκριση με τη συμβατική χειρουργική επέμβαση μετά από ένα χρόνο.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How to Reduce Waste When Renovating Your Home Reading Time: 3 minutes Renovating can make your home work better for you, but stripping out rooms and replacing old materials can create a lot of waste along the way. In England alone, 63.3 million tonnes of non-hazardous construction and demolition waste were generated in 2024, according to UK statistics on waste . Your individual renovation will only represent a tiny part of that picture, but it still makes sense to question what you throw away. Keeping useful features, finding new homes for unwanted materials and buying with longevity in mind can all make a refurbishment less wasteful. Work with what you already have A renovation does not have to start with an empty room. Before removing anything, look at what you already have and decide whether each feature genuinely needs replacing or simply needs some attention. Kitchen units offer a good example. If the carcasses remain sturdy, you could keep them and change the doors or handles instead. Wooden flooring can often be sanded and refinished, while dated furniture may look completely different after a repair or a fresh coat of paint. Keeping existing features can make financial sense too. When you avoid unnecessarily replacing a perfectly usable item, you can put that part of your budget towards improvements that matter more to you. It also helps to separate function from appearance. Something may no longer suit the style you have in mind, but that does not necessarily make it waste. Painting or repairing it could achieve the result you want without buying a brand-new replacement. Find another use for what you remove You will not be able to keep everything, particularly during a larger renovation. However, removing an item from your home does not automatically mean you need to put it in a skip. Doors, cabinets, shelves and unopened building materials could potentially find a second home. You might sell suitable pieces through Facebook Marketplace or eBay, offer them through Freecycle, or contact a local reclamation yard to see what it accepts. Think about this before demolition begins. Once someone throws reusable materials into a skip alongside rubble and broken plasterboard, you may find it much harder to recover them in a usable condition. You can also keep certain leftover materials for future repairs. A few spare bathroom tiles take up very little storage space, for example, but could prove useful if one cracks several years after you finish the renovation. The same applies to a small amount of correctly labelled paint or spare flooring. Be selective about what you replace Sometimes replacing an old fitting is unavoidable. It may leak, perform poorly or simply have reached the end of its useful life. However, renovating gives you an opportunity to think more carefully about what genuinely needs to go. In a kitchen, you might replace damaged worktops while keeping a perfectly usable sink, or change cupboard fronts without removing the units behind them. If you do need new kitchen taps , choosing a style that works with the finished room can sit alongside practical considerations such as water efficiency and build quality. You can use the same thinking throughout your home. A higher-quality fitting that you can maintain or repair may stay in place considerably longer than a cheaper alternative that you have to replace when one component fails. Try to consider the expected lifespan of an item alongside its upfront price. Spending a little more on something durable may reduce the number of times you need to buy, remove and dispose of the same type of product in the future. Avoid creating waste with new materials Renovation waste does not only come from old materials. Ordering too much of something can leave you with boxes of tiles, excess timber or unused flooring once the work finishes. Measure the space carefully before ordering and calculate how much material the project realistically requires. You will usually need to allow some extra for cuts, breakages and mistakes, but that is different from ordering a large surplus simply to be safe. It is worth checking a retailer’s returns policy before you buy as well. If it accepts unused full packs, you have the option of returning excess materials rather than storing them indefinitely or throwing them away. You may also find ways to use smaller leftovers around the home. Timber offcuts could become a shelf, while a handful of spare tiles might be enough for a small splashback or another repair. Creating a more sustainable home is not only about adding new eco-friendly products . Sometimes the greener decision is to keep something for longer, repair what you can and think about where materials will end up before you remove them. With a little more planning, you can still create a home that feels different without treating everything that came before as disposable. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work Reading Time: 4 minutes How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work There are more than 100 million annual bird sightings logged on eBird by observers every day, yet many nature enthusiasts still assume meaningful conservation work requires formal lab credentials and massive institutional budgets. A lingering gap between public curiosity and formal scientific access often leaves local ecosystems unmonitored for years. Citizen science bridges that divide by turning routine outdoor observations into structured ecological data. Worldwide, conservation agencies, universities, and wildlife nonprofits now actively recruit everyday observers to track species shifts, flag habitat loss, and expand research capacity far beyond what small field teams could manage alone. What Citizen Science Is and Why It Matters Citizen science invites members of the public to collect, classify, and share real-world observations with professional researchers. Rather than replacing trained ecologists, public contributors act as an expansive sensory network across neighborhoods, coastlines, and rural landscapes. Small academic teams rarely have the budget to monitor thousands of square miles simultaneously. Volunteers fill those geographic and seasonal blind spots simply by documenting what lives in their backyards or along familiar trails. Even a single timestamped photograph of a blooming wildflower or migrating raptor adds an anchor point to regional biodiversity maps. How Volunteer Data Informs Habitat Protection and Species Management Raw sightings only become useful when researchers can aggregate them into clear ecological patterns. Once uploaded to shared repositories, thousands of individual logs reveal when migratory birds arrive early, where invasive plants are spreading, or which amphibian populations are quietly declining. Wildlife managers rely on these trends to prioritize land acquisition and adjust seasonal protections. Here’s an example. When volunteer records consistently show pollinators clustering along a specific utility corridor, municipal planners gain concrete evidence to preserve that strip instead of mowing it down. Accurate local records turn vague environmental concern into defensible policy decisions. Turning Field Curiosity into a Conservation Career Spending weekends logging water quality or tracking nesting shorebirds frequently changes how people view their own professional lives. Casual curiosity sharpens into methodical questioning once an observer starts noticing why certain species thrive in one creek and vanish from the next. Many volunteers discover they want more than a weekend hobby. Moving from enthusiast to full-time practitioner usually requires structured academic preparation. Inspired participants explore options ranging from technical field certifications to formal biology degree programs that build the scientific foundation needed for careers in wildlife research, environmental policy, and conservation management. Coursework in ecology, genetics, and statistical analysis equips aspiring conservationists to design the very studies they once supported as volunteers. Partnering with Schools, Nonprofits, and Conservation Organizations Individual data collection carries real weight, yet institutional partnerships multiply what a single observer can accomplish. Local schools, land trusts, and watershed coalitions frequently coordinate regional monitoring drives that align volunteer effort with urgent research gaps. Community groups can amplify their conservation footprint through several collaborative pathways: K-12 classrooms adopt nearby streams to submit seasonal macroinvertebrate counts to state environmental agencies Regional land trusts pair amateur naturalists with staff biologists for annual breeding bird inventories Municipal park departments host weekend BioBlitz events to catalog urban tree health and insect diversity University extension offices train community volunteers to monitor invasive species along public trail systems Working inside an organized network ensures that observations follow standardized protocols, making the resulting datasets far more reliable for peer-reviewed analysis. How Community Involvement Builds Local Stewardship People rarely fight to protect landscapes they barely know. Regularly surveying a neighborhood wetland or coastal dune creates an intimate familiarity that abstract news headlines never match. Once residents recognize individual warbler species or spot early signs of soil erosion, conservation stops feeling like someone else’s responsibility. Neighbors begin attending zoning hearings, advocating for native landscaping, and mentoring younger observers. Shared fieldwork transforms passive bystanders into vocal stewards who hold local leaders accountable for environmental decisions. Popular Citizen Science Projects and Monitoring Tools Getting involved does not require specialized laboratory equipment or remote expedition travel. Modern mobile platforms and long-running seasonal counts make participation accessible from almost anywhere. Birdwatchers frequently contribute to global avian databases during annual backyard counts, logging species abundance across winter and spring migrations. Pollinator enthusiasts use dedicated survey protocols to record bumblebee and monarch activity in community gardens. Meanwhile, smartphone wildlife apps allow hikers to snap photos of butterflies , fungi, reptiles, and plants, using computer vision paired with community verification to confirm the identities of species within hours. Measuring Long-Term Conservation Impact Skeptics sometimes wonder whether crowd-sourced observations hold up under rigorous scientific scrutiny. Over the past decade, researchers have developed robust validation frameworks that filter outliers and verify identification accuracy. Recent evaluations show that adaptable volunteer monitoring protocols help conservation scientists respond quickly to shifting ecological priorities without sacrificing data integrity. In marine and coastal regions, international bodies have also established clear quality labeling and sharing standards so community-gathered ocean datasets integrate smoothly into global climate assessments. Longitudinal records spanning ten or twenty years now underpin major habitat restoration grants and endangered species reviews. Getting Started in Your Local Community Stepping into citizen science works best when you start small and stay consistent. Choose a single taxon or local habitat you already enjoy visiting, then commit to observing it across changing seasons. Researchers consistently find that structured community-based biodiversity monitoring yields the strongest conservation value when participants stick with simple, repeatable reporting routines. Choosing a Local Focus Area Start with a nearby park, creek, or backyard garden rather than planning ambitious weekend expeditions. Familiarity with one small patch makes it much easier to spot subtle ecological shifts over time. Learning Basic Observation Protocols Spend twenty minutes reviewing how a project records location, weather, and species counts before submitting your first entry. Clean metadata matters just as much as a sharp photograph when scientists analyze your logs later. Connecting with Regional Coordinators Reach out to a local nature center, watershed alliance, or birding club to ask which datasets regional managers actually need. Aligning your walks with active local priorities ensures your notes solve real conservation problems. Where Everyday Observation Meets Lasting Stewardship Citizen science proves that meaningful environmental protection does not belong exclusively to credentialed specialists. Every careful observation adds another verifiable thread to our collective understanding of changing ecosystems. Whether you stay an active neighborhood volunteer or pursue formal scientific training, consistent attention to the natural world creates tangible momentum for conservation. If this piece was helpful, explore more guides on environmental conservation, field research, and community stewardship across our related articles below. The post How Citizen Science Can Lead to Conservation Work appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A bird following a boat at sea can mean a variety of things to superstitious sailors. They have been seen as harbingers of nearby land, bearers of the souls of the dead or talismans of good luck, among others. Now add this: They deliver data. A group of scientists from the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Spain have wired seabirds with tiny audio recorders and used them as unwitting boat-trackers. The recordings reveal these birds are encountering a lot more vessels on the water than regular vessel-monitoring systems show, according to a paper published today in Science Advances . That insight could help conservationists better protect endangered seabirds from getting killed by fishing nets. “For threatened seabirds,” said Jonathan Rutter , a University of Oxford scientist and the paper’s lead author. “Understanding where they encounter fishing vessels is crucial to protecting them.” Fishing boats can be a magnet for seabirds seeking an easy meal from trapped or discarded fish. But those encounters can prove lethal for animals like the Balearic shearwater , considered Europe’s most endangered seabird . Accidental capture by fishing nets or lines, commonly known as bycatch, is a prime threat to the gull-like brown bird that nests only on Spain’s Balearic Islands in the western Mediterranean Sea. That makes knowing the whereabouts of fishing boats a key part of protecting and recovering such birds. It can help scientist estimate the toll of bycatch, and whether measures such as fishing restrictions are needed. But it’s hard to know how many boats are really on the water. Most large vessels are supposed to carry transponders that continuously signal their location. But there has long been a problem with “invisible” boats, because beacons are turned off or malfunctioning, or sailors eschew the equipment altogether. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , crisscrossed by 1000s of ships that have been virtually invisible. Until now. Some researchers have used satellites to try to solve the problem . But that doesn’t tell scientists how much birds are interacting with these boats. The advent of small, cheap audio recorders and computer programs capable of identifying the acoustic fingerprint of various animals and machines gave Rutter and colleagues another approach. They attached acoustic recorders and tracking devices to seabirds in three different parts of the ocean to see what boats they encountered. In the North Atlantic near the British Isles they used seven northern gannets. In the Mediterranean near the Spanish coast they outfitted four Balearic shearwaters. And in the south Pacific they used a lone Westland petrel. The audio recordings revealed that the birds encountered far more vessels than standard tracking data revealed. The tell-tale drone of ship equipment, compared to vessel tracking records, told the scientists that roughly 57% of the gannets’ ship encounters occurred with vessels that didn’t turn up in normal monitoring systems. For shearwaters, it was around 20%. “We know that seabirds regularly interact with fishing vessels at sea, but what surprised us was just how many of these interactions were missing from conventional tracking records,” said Rutter. The system isn’t perfect. It could be fine-tuned to better distinguish the sounds of fishing boats from other craft. And it wouldn’t work in cases where fishers string lines of hooks stretching dozens of kilometers across the water, far out of earshot of the boat. The method “is not a silver bullet,” the authors write. But it could be “a growing toolbox in which no method provides a complete picture.” So don’t expect flocks of eavesdropping birds to suddenly take to the skies. Then again, these days you never know who’s listening. Rutter et. al. “Unseen but not unheard: Animal-borne audio recorders reveal missing interactions between seabirds and untracked vessels.” Science Advances. Nov. 25, 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: This week’s episode is a short one with a single theme. Arielle takes a few minutes to thank the people who keep pressing play, wherever they happen to be spending this Thursday, from a crowded family table to a Friendsgiving far from home. Stay for a friendly note about The Optimist Daily’s push to welcome 100 new Emissaries before the year is out. Arielle and Karissa are back with a full roundup next week. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Arielle: Hi, everyone. It’s Arielle from The Optimist Daily. No full roundup this week. Karissa and I are taking a little breather, but we didn’t want the week to go by without saying hi and saying thank you. In the US, it’s Thanksgiving week. I know a lot of you aren’t in the US and plenty of you might not celebrate it at all. As longtime listeners know, I’m Canadian, and I live in Amsterdam, so this Thursday is a pretty normal day for me, too. But I love the spirit of Thanksgiving, stopping for a moment to notice what’s good in your life and who helped make it that way. And you don’t need a turkey or a long weekend for that. So here’s what we at The Optimist Daily are grateful for this year. You. Every week, we go looking for people fixing things, like the communities restoring rivers, the teenagers creating education programs for their underserved peers locally and globally, and the cities trying something new to make art and books more accessible. Then we get to share those stories with people who want to hear them. That still feels like a gift. Your messages, your emails, the stories you send our way, the fact that you press play, like, follow, and/or subscribe at all, it means a lot to me and Karissa and the rest of our team. I also have one small ask. The Optimist Daily runs on the support of our Emissaries. They’re the readers and listeners who chip in so we can keep doing this without any paywalls and keep good news out there for everyone. Our goal is to welcome one hundred new Emissaries before the end of the year, and we’re just about at the halfway point. If this show has made your week a little lighter or given you something hopeful to bring up at dinner, we’d love for you to be one of those one hundred. As you plan your year-end donations, becoming an Emissary is a lovely way to say thanks back. And with Giving Tuesday coming up next week, we hope you’ll encourage your circle to support The Optimist Daily, too. You can find the link in the show notes. And if that’s not in the cards for you right now, that’s completely okay. Sharing an episode, an article, or a social media post helps at least one more person add something positive to their day, and that little bit of positivity can turn a whole day around. It’s a chain reaction that starts with something so small, and it’s more powerful than it looks. So thank you again for being part of this Optimist movement. However you’re spending this week, whether it’s at a big table full of family, at a Friendsgiving if you’re away from home, curled up for a quiet night in, or if it’s just another Thursday, I hope you get a moment to feel thankful for something. Karissa and I will be back next week with a full roundup. Until then, take care of each other. Bye for now. items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. City of tomorrow At first glance, the sky seems to be the limit for Utah City, a new community in one of Utah’s fastest-growing cities, with the developer citing the cost of constructing high rises as the only constraint. The development checks all the boxes for the kind of sustainable, pedestrian-first urban living we often cover at RTBC: high density, walkability, green spaces, convenient transit options. And the project is ambitious , expected to be finished in 15 to 20 years. But Utah City faces heavy scrutiny, as Grist and the Salt Lake Tribune report in a story shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby. Though one new resident describes it as “rad” and “vibey,” members of the local city council call it a “gamble,” expressing skepticism that such a community makes sense in a place full of freeways and single-family homes. As one council member put it: “Walkability I don’t care about. [It] forces a lifestyle the average person isn’t living. Most people drive a car.” Becca says: If you build it, will they come? This is a fascinating look at a dense, transit-centered development that seems great on paper but may not be compatible with local desires. Popularity contest Imagine the U.S. without red states or blue states, just millions of people whose votes all matter equally. That’s what would happen if we got rid of the Electoral College, and according to a New York Times opinion piece shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, thanks to this month’s election, this idea is closer than ever to becoming a reality. Now that Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin will have Democratic governors and Democratic majorities in their legislatures, those states may sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. As its name suggests, the compact would make it so that presidential elections are decided by the popular vote. Eighteen states have already adopted it, and if these five sign, writes Jesse Wegman, senior fellow at the Brennan Center for Justice, “then as early as November 2028 we could experience something no one has ever seen — a presidential election in which all Americans’ votes count equally and the candidate who gets the most votes wins.” Will says: I’d been half-listening to the news about states abandoning the Electoral College, but I hadn’t fully absorbed how profoundly this could impact American democracy — in a good way — until I read this piece . What else we’re reading Himalayan Communities Are Relying on Centuries-Old Water Solutions In the Face of Climate Change — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Time Goats vs. vines: Baby goats devour invasive plants, save native trees in Mecklenburg County — shared by Will Doig from WFAE NYC Citi Bike member rides to be capped at $3.65 after Mamdani inks new deal with Lyft — shared by Rebecca Worby from Gothamist From our readers… Earlier this year, we published a story about wild European bison returning to the Carpathian Mountains of southwestern Romania. This week, we heard from Alex at Live Species , a small independent site that shows the latest published count for each of the world’s rarest wild animals, and those, like bison, whose numbers have recovered enough to tick up past 1,000. “The bison page shows none living free in 1927 and 9,762 in free-living herds in December 2024, a head count from the European Bison Pedigree Book,” writes Alex. “The page also credits WWF-Romania and Rewilding Europe for moving bison into the Țarcu Mountains, where they now range free.” Thanks, Alex! The post What We’re Reading: Building a Walkable City From Scratch appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News California Ecohome Wins First Place With a Water-Smart Approach to Landscaping Reading Time: 3 minutes The Arcadia Ecohome Microforest earned top honors in a 2026 landscape contest by combining rainwater and graywater harvesting, drip irrigation, rain gardens, and rewilding practices. In our previous story, we explored how conservation can become something people practice where they live. At the Arcadia Ecohome Microforest in California, that idea extends to one of our most important natural resources: water. This July, the Ecohome was awarded first place in the Upper San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District’s (Upper Water) 2026 Home Landscape Contest as part of Smart Irrigation Month. Smart Irrigation Month is a global campaign the Irrigation Association launched in 2005 to educate homeowners, businesses, growers, and communities about the social, economic, and environmental benefits of water-efficient irrigation. Observed every July, it promotes water efficiency during the peak of summer demand. As backyard growers and homeowners based at the Arcadia Ecohome Microforest, we have supported and participated in the campaign since 2010. Taking part in Smart Irrigation Month 2026 was part of our plan, so we entered Upper Water’s Home Landscape Contest and submitted photos showing how we use smart irrigation practices. On July 31, we learned that the Arcadia Ecohome won first place. Upper Water said the submission demonstrated “thoughtful smart irrigation practices and a strong commitment to water conservation.” The prize was a Smart Flow Monitor Device. For me, the recognition also reflects something I have learned through years of participating in Smart Irrigation Month. A “smart” irrigation system is not a one-size-fits-all solution. It combines and integrates different applications to use available water resources more effectively. We have applied that approach across the Arcadia Ecohome Microforest, where more than 500 trees, shrubs, and vines grow on a half-acre residential lot. The landscape is also a Certified Wildlife Habitat, Certified Pollinator Habitat, and Certified Monarch Waystation. Our water-smart system combines hand watering, deep watering, drip irrigation, rainwater and graywater harvesting, permeable surfaces, forest-floor covering, and distributed rain-garden subsystems. One example is at the main irrigation station serving the rear yard. Alongside a hose bibb and the automatic drip irrigation control station is a repurposed DIY water barrel that collects rainwater from a downspout. Graywater from the Energy Star-rated washing machine in the nearby laundry room and from sinks and tubs in the upstairs main bathroom is also incorporated into the system. These different water sources are integrated into a small rain garden. Drip irrigation pipes run beneath an organic mulch layer of fallen leaves, twigs, and brush around the tree roots. Through “leave-the-leaves” and rewilding practices, we keep organic material on site rather than removing it as waste. The forest-floor layer retains moisture and supports soil biodiversity, while the mulch also helps minimize evaporation from the irrigation system. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, helping plants receive moisture efficiently while reducing unnecessary water use. Photo by Nebular on Unsplash. Water is managed in other parts of the property through a distributed rain-garden system integrated with the irrigation subsystems. One section includes a rainwater harvesting system with a downspout, a DIY water barrel, and a rain garden with both manual and automatic irrigation lines. Rocks and gravel create a flow channel that carries overflow from the rain barrel into the garden. The goal is not simply to water plants. It is to make use of different water resources while supporting a landscape that functions as habitat. That approach has also allowed the Ecohome to educate the community. Because the property adjoins Camino Grove and Camino Grove Park and receives considerable foot traffic, I installed educational signage in the front yard to raise public awareness of the landscape’s features. The top of the sign features an “Ocean Friendly Garden” designation awarded by the Surfrider Foundation for conservation, permeability, stormwater retention, and reduced urban runoff pollution in water bodies. The Ecohome has also hosted voluntary educational workshops and tours and supported awareness campaigns, including World Water Week, World Water Day, World Water Monitoring Day, Fix-A-Leak Week, and Smart Irrigation Month. In June 2012, our community partner, the Chinese American Construction Professionals (CACP), joined us for a grassroots workshop and tour at the Ecohome in support of Smart Irrigation Month. More recently, a workshop and tour on July 26, 2025, brought together guests, volunteers, and news reporters in the Ecohome’s permeable front yard. The event was later featured by the Epoch Times and SingTao Daily. The first-place award from Upper Water is meaningful because it recognizes an approach we have been developing at the Ecohome for years. More importantly, it gives us another opportunity to show that water conservation doesn’t have to be separate from habitat creation, rewilding, or community education. A residential landscape can capture rainwater, reuse graywater, reduce evaporation, manage stormwater, support wildlife, and give people a place to learn. For me, that is what makes an irrigation system truly smart: not one solution working alone, but different practices working together to make better use of the water and resources already around us. The post California Ecohome Wins First Place With a Water-Smart Approach to Landscaping appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Floating Wetlands Cut Wastewater Emissions in Australian Treatment Lagoons Reading Time: 3 minutes A world-first trial in Australia found that floating wetlands made of native reeds cut greenhouse gas emissions from a wastewater lagoon by up to 36%. Floating wetlands built from native reeds and sedges have cut greenhouse gas emissions from a wastewater lagoon by more than a quarter. A two-year trial on Phillip Island in southeastern Australia tracked the results continuously using solar-powered sensors. Researchers call it the first real-world test at full operational scale. RMIT University led the trial with Westernport Water, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization, and Deakin University. Wastewater treatment already accounts for about 1.6 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. That share is expected to grow as more countries improve access to sanitation. Scientists floated a platform of native plants roughly the size of one and a half tennis courts on part of a treatment lagoon. Plant roots dangled directly into the water below. A second, untreated section of the same lagoon served as a comparison point throughout the study. The lagoon itself held roughly 14 million liters of wastewater at the Westernport Water treatment site. High nutrient levels in wastewater create ideal conditions for the microbes that generate greenhouse gases in the first place. Floating wetlands aim to interrupt that cycle by giving plants and their root microbes a foothold directly on the water’s surface. Carbon dioxide emissions from the floating wetland section dropped by up to 36% compared to the untreated lagoon. Methane fell by up to 66%, and nitrous oxide emissions fell by up to 18%. Combined, overall greenhouse gas emissions fell by roughly 31%. Researchers expected floating wetlands to help mainly by removing nutrients from the water over time. Instead, emissions began dropping within four to seven months, well before nutrient levels changed much. That gap surprised the research team and remains only partly understood. Scientists suspect the roots host microbial communities that interact with the gases in ways we still don’t fully understand. Testing those interactions directly will take further research. For now, the emissions drop stands as a real-world result even without a confirmed explanation; one researcher plans to keep investigating as the technology moves toward wider use. Some treatment plants already use floating wetlands to soak up excess nitrogen and phosphorus before discharging or reusing water. This trial adds emissions reduction to that established role. The approach requires no major new infrastructure, since existing lagoons can be retrofitted directly. Floating wetlands now tackle greenhouse gas emissions alongside their established role in removing nitrogen and phosphorus from wastewater, with existing treatment lagoons retrofitted directly and no major new infrastructure required. Photo courtesy of ScienceDirect . Some practical details still need attention before wider rollout. Trimming the plants keeps them healthy and boosts nutrient uptake, but cutting also triggers short bursts of methane release. Researchers are working out how to manage that trade-off without losing the overall benefit. The trial produced nearly one metric ton of harvested plant material over its run. Turning that material into biochar could lock its carbon away for the long term. Without that step, some of the climate benefits could eventually be undone. Building on these results, researchers are now testing floating wetlands on farm dams in Victoria’s Bass Coast region. According to the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization, Australia has roughly 1.8 million farm dams that could potentially benefit from the same approach. Farm dams often receive heavy loads of nutrients and organic matter from livestock, which can drive their own emissions. Water utilities worldwide have few affordable options for cutting emissions from open-air lagoons today. Most existing fixes involve covering ponds or installing mechanical treatment systems, both of which are expensive. A planted, low-maintenance platform offers a much cheaper starting point for utilities on tight budgets. If floating wetlands prove effective across different water bodies, they could offer a low-tech tool for cutting emissions at a global scale. The approach works with existing infrastructure rather than requiring costly rebuilds. For a sector still searching for affordable climate solutions, that combination of simplicity and results may be exactly what’s needed. The post Floating Wetlands Cut Wastewater Emissions in Australian Treatment Lagoons appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When a writer moved to a small Vermont town and began helping elders record their life stories, what emerged was far more than local history -- it was evidence of something science now confirms: that storytelling is, at its core, a biological act of human bonding, one that physically synchronizes the brains of speaker and listener. Oral historian Esther Ehrlich found herself falling in love with every single person she interviewed -- even the medical malpractice insurance executive she'd initially dreaded meeting. She notes that "oral histories, at their most basic, include all the stuff that makes us people, including our desire to be seen, heard, and understood." Holocaust survivor Helen Marks has watched thousands of students be moved in ways no textbook could achieve, and hospice volunteer Neal Allen discovered that helping the dying retrieve long-buried memories wasn't sorrowful work but "quite extraordinary." What sharing stories quietly insists is that every life, told honestly, becomes a gift -- not only to those who receive it, but to the person finally brave enough to offer it.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News From Fly Larvae to Soup Kitchens: Local Ideas for Reducing Food Loss and Waste Globally Reading Time: 3 minutes Schools in Nairobi, soup kitchens in Lima, and market vendors in Quezon City show what works in reducing food loss and waste globally. Reducing food loss and waste globally is one of the most direct ways to feed people and cut emissions. About 13% of food is lost between harvest and retail. Another 19% of the food that reaches consumers is wasted in shops, restaurants, and homes. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) put a number on that waste in its 2024 Food Waste Index. In 2022, the world threw away about 1.05 billion tonnes of food, or roughly one billion meals a day. That same year, 783 million people went hungry. Households wasted the most, about 631 million tonnes. The average person wasted 79 kilograms of food that year, about the weight of an adult. Wasted food also harms the climate. Food loss and waste produce up to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions. That is almost five times the emissions from aviation. The United Nations marks the International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste every September 29. The 2026 theme focused on the transformative potential of cutting both. For CGIAR, a global network of agricultural research centers, the day was a chance to rethink the problem. Dr. Mukani Moyo leads urban food systems research in CGIAR’s Food Frontiers and Security Program. She argues that losses often begin on farms, long before food reaches a city. In her view, cities cannot tackle waste without looking upstream. Perishable crops show why. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) lists fruits, vegetables, roots, and tubers among the foods most at risk. For example, rough handling, poor storage, and weak market links often cause potatoes and sweet potatoes to be lost. The fixes are practical. Better-adapted crop varieties, improved storage, and local processing all help. Solar-powered cold storage can keep produce fresh in places with little electricity. In Nairobi, schoolchildren are tackling the problem from the other end of the chain. At three schools and a farmers’ hub, they feed lunch leftovers and kitchen scraps to black soldier fly larvae. Raised in containers called biopods, the larvae eat organic waste quickly and grow rich in protein. The World Vegetable Center and the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture lead the project. Each biopod started in mid-2026 with 3 kilograms of young larvae. The first harvests at the schools weighed 15 to 19 kilograms each. In the second cycle, larvae production rose by 30 to 60%. Farmers feed the larvae to pigs and poultry, and one farmer reports her pigs compete eagerly for them. The leftover material, called frass, goes back to school gardens as fertilizer. Black soldier fly larvae turn lunch scraps into animal feed, a small step toward reducing food loss and waste globally. Photo by Rodrick rajive lal on Wikimedia Commons This matters in Africa, where up to 40% of food is lost or wasted along informal urban supply chains. Projects like this show how reducing food loss and waste globally can start in a single schoolyard. Lima, Peru, takes a different approach. Community food rescue groups collect surplus food from local producers. They pass it on to ollas comunes, community soup kitchens that feed families in low-income neighborhoods. Researchers from the International Potato Center have studied these kitchens as a source of community resilience. Food that might have spoiled instead becomes nutritious meals. Vietnamese farmers are closing the loop on their own land. They compost livestock manure and crop leftovers, returning the nutrients to their fields. That cuts waste and reduces the need to buy fertilizer. Ghanaian researchers are studying how to turn large volumes of city food waste back into farm inputs. The goal is to scale promising local solutions beyond small pilots. In Quezon City, Philippines, the Vendor Business School trains vegetable vendors in safe food handling and business skills. It also teaches them to cope with heat that spoils produce. The program started in 2024 with 140 vendors. City leaders saw enough value to make it permanent. A 2025 city ordinance now writes the Vendor Business School into local law. Vendors report more confidence and more repeat customers. Japan has cut its food waste by 18%, and the United Kingdom by 31%. Both offer models for reducing food loss and waste globally. The UN aims to halve food waste by 2030. Moyo stresses that technology alone will not succeed in reducing food loss and waste globally. Scaling up requires finance, infrastructure, skills, and better research on where and why food is lost. It also requires farmers, traders, businesses, and city governments to work together. Local context matters most. A solution that works in Nairobi may need changes before it works in Accra or Lima. Reducing food loss and waste globally will depend on many local answers, each fitted to its place. The post From Fly Larvae to Soup Kitchens: Local Ideas for Reducing Food Loss and Waste Globally appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. What does peace taste like? At the 20th World Summit of Nobel Peace Laureates, held in Rome from December 1 to 4, Miki Kawamura plans to let visitors decide for themselves. PeaceCream, a pop-up she has developed through her Youth Peace Ambassadors program in collaboration with Japan’s Goi Peace Foundation , gives each ice cream flavor a value tied to peace, such as love, hope, gratitude, or compassion. Participants think about what peace means to them, then build their own cup from the flavors and toppings that represent the values they want to bring into the world. “What if we could make peace something people can taste, feel, and share?” Miki asked when she described the idea to The Optimist Daily . The concept is playful, but the conviction behind it runs through everything Miki has built since she was 18. In her view, peace has been left too long to political debates and international institutions. “It should become a part of our everyday lives, something we can experience, practice, and create together,” she said. Youth Peace Ambassadors begins with the individual A boarding school with students from 80 countries Miki graduated in 2025 from UWC ISAK Japan, an international boarding school in rural Japan whose students come from more than 80 countries. Living alongside classmates from so many backgrounds taught her that peace grows less from agreement than from a common aim, a lesson she later laid out in a DailyGood essay titled “I’m 18. Here’s What I’ve Learned About Peace.” As she put it there, “Our differences may sometimes divide us, but a shared desire for peace has the power to bring us back.” From one gap year to more than 100 countries She founded Youth Peace Ambassadors in June 2025, during a gap year that also included an internship at the Goi Peace Foundation , one of Japan’s longest-running peace organizations. The premise is that peace is something each person works on internally before building it with anyone else. Within a year, the network had grown to more than 2,000 members between the ages of 14 and 30, spread across more than 100 countries and connected by that shared aim instead of any political position. Dot Maver, a World Business Academy Fellow who nominated Miki for this series, has watched the approach up close. “Miki has dedicated herself to realizing Peace in herself, and inspiring others to do the same, and then to put Peace in Action in communities around the world,” Maver wrote. “It matters to me as a Peacebuilder who recognizes that peace begins with each one of us.” The Global Youth Peace Journey 1,592 applicants and a three percent acceptance rate In 2026, Miki launched the Peace Journey, a youth peace education program that invites participants to find their own path to peace through their passions, dreams, and fields of interest. It drew 1,592 applications from 104 countries, and only about three percent of applicants were accepted, according to Miki’s DailyGood essay. Maver served as a guide for the cohort. The same year, Miki hosted a Ripples of Peace Retreat in London, presented at the Goi Peace Foundation Forum, and spoke at a Community of Living Ethics Conference in Italy. Maver, who was there, wrote that Miki “touched hearts and minds of all ages” and called her “a living demonstration of peace in action.” Peace Journey 2027 applications open in December The next Peace Journey begins in January 2027, with applications expected to open in early December. What Miki values most about the program is the permission it gives young people to start now. Participants learn, she said, that “they do not need to wait until they have extraordinary resources, influence, or experience to make a difference.” Peace, in her framing, can begin with who you are, how you treat others and what you choose to do today. Youth peacebuilding from Rome to Japan PeaceCream’s international debut The Rome pop-up will be PeaceCream’s first appearance in front of an international audience, at a summit whose 2026 theme centers on artificial intelligence and peace. Miki hopes the experience sparks conversations between strangers and connects people across their differences, using one of the most universally loved foods as an entry point. “Our vision is to make peace not just something we talk about, but something we experience and want to share with others,” she said. Four ambassadors return to the Goi Peace Foundation Closer to home, four Youth Peace Ambassadors will travel to Japan for the Goi Peace Foundation’s annual forum and summit to share the projects they developed during the Peace Journey and compare notes on turning their ideas into action. Miki sees the gathering as a chance to link the ambassadors’ separate initiatives and show more young people that they can lead change themselves. Miki began her undergraduate studies at Minerva University this fall and has brought the network with her, which means Youth Peace Ambassadors now grows alongside a student still working out her own questions about peace in public, much as her essay did. Her aim is to make peace something anyone can take part in, regardless of age, background, or circumstance, and the upcoming Peace Journey is the most direct way to do that. Young readers who want to apply can find the application, once it opens in December, on the Youth Peace Ambassadors website . The post Miki Kawamura: a 19-year-old’s peace network brings ice cream to a Nobel summit first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Οι περισσότεροι επίμονοι λεκέδες στα ρούχα είναι ένα πρόβλημα χημείας και η επιδιόρθωση εξαρτάται από την αντιστοίχιση της θεραπείας με το μόριο. Τα λίπη χρειάζονται ένζυμα που αφομοιώνουν το λίπος, οι φυτικές χρωστικές διασπώνται κάτω από το υπεριώδες φως και η συσσώρευση ορυκτών διαλύεται σε ήπιο οξύ. Λάθος η σύζευξη και ο λεκές μπορεί να σταθεροποιηθεί μόνιμα. Έρικ Τομπ…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most stubborn laundry stains are a chemistry problem, and the fix depends on matching the treatment to the molecule. Fats need fat-digesting enzymes, plant pigments break down under ultraviolet light, and mineral buildup dissolves in mild acid. Get the pairing wrong, and the stain can set permanently. Eric Thompson, a former management consultant near Seattle who moderates the r/laundry forum on Reddit, has seen it happen. “If you pour vinegar on a burrito grease stain on white nylon, you now have orange nylon for eternity,” he said. “Acids bind colour to dye sites on nylon.” His forum, with roughly 995,000 members, has become a clearinghouse for evidence-based fixes, and Thompson’s long technical guides on enzymes and citric acid rinses are among its most cited posts. “I don’t do hacks,” he says. “What I do is: ‘Let’s use biotech and green chemistry and the magic of water and time to gently take care of our clothes.'” The payoff goes beyond clean shirts. Clothes that last longer need replacing less often, which saves money and cuts textile waste. Before trying any of the methods below, check care labels, follow safety instructions on household chemicals, and never combine products without confirming it’s safe. Most of these techniques are designed for cotton and polyester. Enzymes and stubborn laundry stains Lipases for cooking oil Enzymes are the “bio” in biological detergents, and each type targets a different molecule. For grease from cooking oil, the enzyme to look for is lipase, which breaks down fats. Many detergents contain it, though packaging often lists only “enzymes,” so checking the manufacturer’s ingredient information can help. Clare Mahon , a professor of polymer chemistry at Durham University whose lab has partnered with a major detergent maker on laundry research, recommends a pretreatment first: a paste of baking soda and water applied to the oily patch for about an hour. “Fats or oils contain ester linkages and that mixture can hydrolyse those,” she said, meaning the paste breaks the bonds down with water. “Then you get water-soluble products that can then be removed from the fabric.” Speed matters here. Over time, the lipids in oil oxidize and link together in ways baking soda can’t undo, “so the stains can be really persistent,” Mahon said. DNase for gym clothes that won’t stop smelling Workout gear that smells clean out of the wash but sour once it warms up has a nickname online: permastank. The culprit is a buildup of body oils and bacteria. One enzyme rarely found in standard detergents, deoxyribonuclease, or DNase, targets extracellular DNA, a material that has no smell itself but helps glue other grime to fabric. Steve Brown, a product designer in Sydney, ran into the problem with his Brazilian jiujitsu gear before developing a DNase-based booster. “I just couldn’t get the smell out of my rash guards; I had to throw a couple of them out,” he said. Solvents, sunlight and acids Oil-based solvents for bike grease Black grease from a bike chain behaves differently from cooking oil. Mahon suggests spraying it with a light oil-based solvent and leaving it for about 10 minutes before washing. “Because it’s a more oily organic solvent, it can release the residue from the fabric a bit more, then the surfactants are able to lift it up in the wash,” she said. Surfactants are the molecules in detergent that bind to dirt and make it water-soluble, which is why an enzyme stain remover alone can’t replace detergent. Sunlight for tomato sauce Red sauce stains often get their color from lycopene, a pigment whose chemical bonds break down under UV light. After pretreating any grease with dish soap and washing as usual, drying the garment outside can fade lingering orange marks completely, even on an overcast day. Citric acid for armpit stains and rough towels Yellowed, stiff underarm patches come from a combination of sweat and deodorant, and Mahon calls them “a nightmare.” Soaking the area in water and citric acid can help dissolve aluminum deposits left by antiperspirant, though it can take several washes. Oxygen-based stain removers can help too, but leaving them on too long can lighten colored fabric. Citric acid also helps with towels that dry scratchy, especially in homes without a tumble dryer. Stiffness often comes from using too much detergent, hard water, or both. Fabric softener isn’t the answer, since it coats fibers and reduces absorbency. Thompson prefers a rinse with dissolved citric acid in the softener compartment. “I am a huge proponent of using citric acid in the rinse,” he said. It binds to the calcium in hard water and neutralizes the alkaline pH that detergent leaves behind. Shaking towels sharply before hanging them also helps lift the fibers. A repeat cycle for sunscreen Sunscreen stains are among the hardest to shift. Many come from chemical UV filters such as avobenzone, which reacts with metal ions in water that then oxidize into a yellow mark. A rust stain remover can reverse the oxidation, but the metal stays in the fabric, and the stain can return as it dries. Thompson’s approach is a cycle of “pretreating, waiting, washing, rust-removing, and then washing again.” Machine care and the last-resort deep clean Cleaning the washer itself A smelly washing machine will pass its odor on to everything in it. Manufacturers recommend a monthly cleaning cycle on the hottest setting, wiping out the rubber door seal, and periodically emptying and rinsing the drain pump filter, which collects lint, plastic, paper, and residue. Polyquat spots Some mystery marks appear only after washing. These are often polyquat stains, caused by polyquaterniums , polymers found in hair products, contact lens solution and children’s bubble mix. In the wash, they attract dirt and dye to the fabric, which effectively turns that patch into a color-catcher sheet, Mahon explained. Color-remover products can sometimes help, but they don’t work on indigo, so a polyquat spot that picked up dye from jeans is likely permanent. Thompson’s “spa day” For persistent odors and dinginess, Thompson’s forum is known for a long, enzyme-powered soak he calls a spa day. Items soak in water with a measured amount of enzyme detergent, held at around 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for several hours, before a regular wash; he also adds household ammonia for degreasing. Ammonia must never be mixed with chlorine bleach, since the combination releases a toxic gas. “It’s incumbent on all of us to keep textiles in the productive-use space as long as possible,” Thompson said. “Spa day is the last-ditch effort to do so when previous care has failed.” None of this needs to become a weekly routine. Overwashing wears out fabric, and shorter cycles at lower temperatures use less energy. Thompson calls a regular mixed load “good enough” for most days, and Mahon thinks the bigger risk may be overthinking it. “To be honest with you, most people’s clothes aren’t actually that dirty,” she said. The chemistry becomes useful on the days a favorite shirt seems ruined, when knowing which molecule caused the stain can decide whether it goes back in the drawer or into the trash. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Austin Energy Rebates and Grid Strain Affect What Homeowners Pay to Cool Their Homes, and How to Qualify for Rebates Reading Time: 4 minutes How Austin Energy Rebates and Grid Strain Affect What Homeowners Pay to Cool Their Homes, and How to Qualify for Rebates On a hot Austin afternoon, the room with the west-facing windows can feel like a different house. The thermostat may read 76°F in the hallway while the air conditioner runs steadily and the room still feels warm. That familiar problem connects three things homeowners can act on: how much heat gets indoors, how much electricity it takes to remove it, and what happens when thousands of air conditioners are running at the same time. Austin’s municipal utility offers rebates for qualifying cooling equipment and improvements such as attic insulation and duct sealing. During a heat wave, longer AC run times can raise the monthly electric bill, while a qualifying Austin Energy rebate can lower the upfront cost of an upgrade that helps the home stay cool with less electricity. Where to start depends on what is driving the cooling load in the first place. What Grid Strain Means for an Austin Electric Bill During a stretch of extreme heat, air conditioners run longer across much of Texas. That raises demand on the grid managed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT. For most Austin Energy households, the immediate effect on the bill comes from using more kilowatt-hours. The utility’s standard residential energy charge has four usage tiers, so electricity used above a monthly threshold is billed at the higher rate for that tier. A heat wave can increase the bill both by extending AC run times and by pushing some of that extra usage into a higher tier. Wholesale power costs can also affect what households pay over time through Austin Energy’s Power Supply Adjustment. This per-kilowatt-hour charge reflects costs such as fuel and electricity bought from the grid. The standard residential bill uses monthly consumption and published rates, so hourly wholesale price spikes affect households indirectly through the utility’s power supply costs. On your own bill, start by comparing kilowatt-hours with the same billing period last year. The dollar total alone makes it harder to tell how much of the change came from electricity use. Which Cooling Rebate Fits the Work Your Home Needs? When an older system is nearing replacement, Eco Air Conditioning’s guide to Austin Energy rebates ⁠ explains how efficient AC equipment and heat pumps can help reduce cooling demand during periods of grid strain. Austin Energy’s published standalone incentive table lists $600 to $800 for qualifying central split or mini-split AC systems and $650 to $950 for qualifying heat pumps, depending on the equipment and efficiency ratings. Ask the contractor to identify the rebate tier for the exact system on the estimate so you can compare the installed price after the expected rebate. If the old system still works but some rooms are consistently hotter than others, a home energy assessment can help identify where the house is gaining heat or losing cooled air. Austin Energy’s Home Energy Savings program takes this broader approach. A participating contractor conducts a no-cost assessment, and the program requires at least three qualifying improvements. The work may include air and duct sealing, attic insulation or solar screens for eligible windows. A replacement system can also be part of the project when it meets the program’s requirements. How to Qualify Before You Commit to an Installation For the standalone equipment rebate, the home must receive electricity from Austin Energy, and both the home and the system being replaced must be at least 10 years old. The program covers replacements, and the existing equipment must not have received an Austin Energy rebate within the past 10 years. A participating contractor must install a qualifying system. Before signing, have the contractor confirm that the proposed equipment meets the applicable efficiency requirements and that the quote covers the system components required by the program. The contractor must document that the equipment was sized for the home and submit the rebate application within 90 days of installation. The homeowner must also agree to a post-installation inspection. Keep an itemized invoice and ask for the application confirmation so you can track its status. For households looking for help with insulation or duct repairs, Austin Energy also offers a separate Weatherization Assistance program that provides eligible customers with home efficiency improvements at no cost. Shade and Insulation Help Before the AC Switches On The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ⁠ explains that trees and other vegetation can cool urban areas and reduce air-conditioning demand by shading buildings. At home, that can start with noticing which windows take the strongest afternoon sun. An exterior screen can reduce solar heat gain at a window, while a well-placed tree can provide shade as it grows. Insulation slows heat transfer through the attic, and sealed ducts help cooled air reach the rooms it was meant for. The environmental benefit extends beyond any one property. When homes gain less heat, they need less electricity to stay comfortable. Across a neighborhood, those savings can help ease peak demand on hot afternoons. They can also reduce greenhouse gas emissions when the electricity saved would otherwise have come from fossil fuels. Shade adds a benefit outside the house, too, by helping cool the spaces around buildings. Use Last Summer’s Bills to Decide Where to Start Pull up a few bills from the hottest months and note which rooms were hard to keep cool. Bring both observations to the contractor. If the equipment is nearing the end of its life, compare qualifying replacements by their installed price after the rebate and ask how much electricity the contractor expects each system to use under similar conditions. If the system still runs well, an assessment can help you decide whether insulation, duct repairs or shading would address the discomfort first. Either way, the aim is a home that stays comfortable through the hottest part of the day with less electricity. The post How Austin Energy Rebates and Grid Strain Affect What Homeowners Pay to Cool Their Homes, and How to Qualify for Rebates appeared first on Happy Eco News .
