items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Home Solar Batteries Work, What They Cost and How They Add Resilience During Outages Reading Time: 3 minutes How Home Solar Batteries Work, What They Cost and How They Add Resilience During Outages Rooftop solar panels have become a familiar sight, but more homeowners are now asking a second question: what happens to all that solar energy when the sun goes down, or when the power goes out? Home batteries are the answer for a growing number of households. They store electricity for later use, help homeowners use more of their own clean energy and keep essential appliances running during outages. Here is how home solar batteries work, what affects their cost and why they are becoming an important part of a more resilient, sustainable home. How a Solar Battery System Works Solar panels produce direct current electricity when sunlight hits them. An inverter converts that power into alternating current, which is what household appliances use. During the day, the home uses solar power first. Without a battery, any extra electricity is usually sent back to the grid. With home solar batteries , that extra daytime energy is stored instead. After sunset, or on cloudy days, the battery supplies stored power through the inverter to run lights, appliances and electronics, and in some setups it can even help fcharge an electric vehicle. Batteries can also be charged from the grid, which is useful for homes without solar or for utility programs that reward shifting electricity use away from peak hours. Backup Power When the Grid Goes Down Resilience is one of the main reasons homeowners install batteries. When the grid fails, a properly configured system detects the outage and switches to stored energy automatically, often so quickly that lights barely flicker. The refrigerator keeps running, phones and laptops stay charged and lights stay on. Most residential batteries are designed to power essential circuits rather than an entire home indefinitely. During installation, homeowners usually choose which loads are connected, such as the fridge, internet router, some lighting, a well pump or a furnace fan. With solar panels recharging the battery during the day, a home can keep critical systems running through longer outages. This kind of resilience is increasingly valuable as storms, wildfires and extreme weather put more pressure on electricity grids. An Environmental Win Home batteries also support a cleaner energy system. By storing solar energy produced during the day and using it in the evening, households rely less on electricity generated during peak hours, which in many regions is when fossil fuel power plants are most likely to run. Utilities can also use networks of home batteries to balance demand on the grid, reducing the need to build new peaking power plants. For homeowners, a battery means using more of the clean energy their own roof produces instead of exporting it and buying power back later. Combined with energy efficiency upgrades and electrified heating and transportation, solar and storage help shrink a household’s carbon footprint and support the wider transition to renewable energy. What Home Batteries Cost Battery costs vary widely depending on the size of the battery, the brand, the installation complexity and whether solar panels are installed at the same time. In British Columbia, BC Hydro estimates that the average cost of a lithium-ion solar battery system and installation ranges from about $18,000 to $25,000 for a residential home. Capacity is the biggest factor. Batteries are measured in kilowatt-hours, and a larger battery can power more circuits for longer. Some homes add electrical upgrades, such as a new panel or a dedicated backup sub-panel, which also affect the price. Rebates and Incentives Incentives can reduce the upfront cost. In British Columbia, BC Hydro offers rebates for eligible solar panels and battery storage systems. Residential battery rebates are available, with higher amounts of up to $5,000 for batteries enrolled in its Peak Saver program, which lets the utility draw on stored energy at times of high demand. Solar panel installations may qualify for a separate rebate of up to $5,000. Program rules, eligible products and contractor requirements change from time to time, so it is worth checking current details before buying. Other provinces and states offer their own incentives, and some utilities provide reduced rates or credits for customers who let them use battery capacity during peak periods. Is a Battery Right for You A battery makes the most sense for homes that already have or plan to install solar panels, experience frequent outages, rely on electricity for heating or medical equipment, or want to maximize their use of renewable energy. Homeowners should consider how much backup power they need, which circuits matter most and how long they would like to stay powered during an outage. A qualified installer can review your electricity use, roof and electrical panel, recommend an appropriate battery size and help with permits and rebate applications. Learn More Natural Resources Canada offers information on renewable energy, home energy efficiency and programs that can help Canadians reduce their energy use. Powering a More Resilient Future Home solar batteries turn rooftop panels into a more complete energy system. They store clean power, keep essential appliances running during outages and help support a greener grid. With falling technology costs and available incentives, more homeowners are finding that a battery is a practical step toward both resilience and sustainability. The post How Home Solar Batteries Work, What They Cost and How They Add Resilience During Outages appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Common Contaminants in Private Well Water, How to Test for Them and How Treatment Protects Health Reading Time: 3 minutes Common Contaminants in Private Well Water, How to Test for Them and How Treatment Protects Health. For millions of rural households, the tap is connected not to a municipal system but to a private well. Well water can be clean, fresh and reliable, but it comes with a responsibility city residents rarely think about. No utility tests it, treats it or monitors it. That job belongs to the owner. Many contaminants have no taste, smell or colour, so water that looks perfect can still carry health risks. Knowing what to watch for, how to test and how treatment works helps keep families safe. Why Well Water Needs Attention Groundwater moves through soil and rock, picking up minerals and, sometimes, contaminants along the way. Activities on the surface, such as farming, septic systems, roads and industry, can affect water quality. Changes such as flooding, drought or nearby construction can shift conditions underground. Because of this, a well that tested clean years ago is not guaranteed to stay that way, and knowing the most common well water contaminants helps owners decide what to test for. Bacteria Bacteria are among the most common concerns. Total coliform bacteria indicate that surface water or soil may be entering the well, while E. coli points to contamination from human or animal waste. Drinking contaminated water can cause stomach illness, and some bacteria pose serious risks for children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems. Bacteria can enter through cracked well caps, poor seals, flooding or a nearby septic system that is not working properly. Nitrates and Nitrites Nitrates and nitrites often come from fertilizers, manure and septic systems. High levels are especially risky for infants, because nitrates can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Wells in agricultural areas or close to septic fields are more likely to be affected. Arsenic and Other Metals Arsenic occurs naturally in some rock formations and can dissolve into groundwater. It has no taste, smell or colour, and long-term exposure is linked to serious health effects. Contaminants like arsenic are important to understand precisely because they cannot be detected without testing. Other metals, such as manganese, uranium and lead from plumbing , can also be present depending on local geology and the age of the home’s pipes. Iron, Manganese and Hardness Some contaminants are mainly nuisance issues. Iron and manganese cause orange or black stains on fixtures and laundry and can give water a metallic taste. Hard water, caused by calcium and magnesium, leaves scale on taps, kettles and water heaters and reduces the effectiveness of soap. While these are not usually health hazards at typical levels, they can shorten the life of appliances and plumbing. Changes in pH can also matter. Acidic water can corrode pipes and release metals into drinking water. How Often to Test Regular testing is the only way to know what is in your water. A common recommendation is to test for bacteria at least once a year and to test for chemicals and metals every few years. Test right away after flooding, construction near the well, repairs to the well or any noticeable change in taste, smell, colour or clarity. Testing is also important when buying or selling a rural property, when someone in the household is pregnant or when treatment equipment is installed or adjusted. Use an accredited laboratory and follow its sampling instructions carefully. Many regional health authorities can recommend labs and help interpret results. How Treatment Protects Health Once you know what is in the water, the right treatment can address it. Ultraviolet disinfection systems kill bacteria and viruses without adding chemicals. Carbon filters reduce certain chemicals, odours and tastes. Specialized filters remove iron and manganese. Water softeners reduce hardness. Reverse osmosis systems, often installed at the kitchen tap, can lower levels of arsenic, nitrates and many dissolved contaminants in drinking water. The best systems are designed around test results, not guesses. Treatment equipment also needs regular maintenance, such as replacing UV lamps, filters and membranes, to keep working properly. Protecting Groundwater for the Future Private wells are directly connected to the environment around them, which makes protecting groundwater a shared responsibility. Maintaining septic systems, using fertilizers and pesticides carefully, storing fuels and chemicals safely and properly sealing unused wells all help keep aquifers clean. Choosing treatment systems that use less water and energy, and recycling or responsibly disposing of filters and equipment, can reduce the environmental footprint of clean drinking water. Healthy groundwater supports not only the households that rely on it, but also streams, wetlands and wildlife across rural regions. Health Canada provides guidance on drinking water quality, including information for private well owners. Clean Water, Peace of Mind Well water can be safe and healthy, but it requires regular attention. Testing on a schedule, understanding the results and choosing the right treatment protect your family’s health and the groundwater your home depends on. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News From Family Reunions to Group Getaways: Exploring Sustainable Whitewater Rafting Adventures Reading Time: 10 minutes From Family Reunions to Group Getaways: Exploring Sustainable Whitewater Rafting Adventures Traveling together has long been a way for families, friends, and colleagues to strengthen relationships, but the nature of group vacations is changing. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional resorts, sightseeing tours, and organized entertainment, many travelers are seeking experiences that encourage meaningful interaction and shared accomplishment. Whitewater rafting offers a compelling alternative by combining outdoor exploration, physical activity, and teamwork in an environment that feels removed from everyday obligations. Participants navigate changing river conditions, encounter dramatic natural landscapes, and experience moments of excitement that cannot easily be replicated through traditional vacation activities. The result is an adventure in which the journey itself becomes the central attraction, creating opportunities for connection across different ages and backgrounds. One of the defining characteristics of whitewater rafting is its ability to bring people together around a common objective. Unlike activities that allow participants to remain relatively independent, rafting requires passengers to communicate, coordinate their movements, and respond collectively to instructions from their guide. A successful run through a series of rapids becomes a shared accomplishment, while calmer stretches offer opportunities for conversation and appreciation of the surrounding environment. This combination of excitement and relaxation makes rafting particularly appealing to groups whose members have different personalities and recreational interests. Even participants who approach the trip with some hesitation often discover that contributing to a team can be just as rewarding as the thrill of navigating moving water. The appeal extends beyond adrenaline, particularly as travelers increasingly place greater value on experiences that bring people closer to nature. Rivers offer access to landscapes that may be difficult to appreciate from roads, established hiking trails, or heavily visited tourist destinations. Forested canyons, rocky gorges, wildlife habitats, and remote stretches of wilderness create an atmosphere that encourages participants to disconnect from digital distractions. Many rafting destinations also provide opportunities for camping, hiking, swimming in designated areas, and exploring nearby communities. For groups planning reunions, celebrations, or recreational retreats, this variety helps transform a rafting excursion into a more complete outdoor vacation. Choosing the Right Whitewater Rafting Experience for Your Group Selecting an appropriate rafting trip begins with understanding the capabilities, expectations, and comfort levels of everyone involved. Across the American West, rivers such as California’s American River, Oregon’s Rogue River, and Idaho’s Salmon River offer different combinations of whitewater difficulty, scenery, and opportunities for group adventures. Whitewater rivers are commonly classified according to the International Scale of River Difficulty, ranging from relatively gentle Class I waters to extremely challenging Class VI conditions. Class II trips often appeal to beginners and families seeking manageable excitement, while Class III sections introduce larger waves and more coordinated paddling. More demanding Class IV and V rapids generally require greater preparation and a higher tolerance for risk. Because river classifications do not guarantee safety, organizers should also consider seasonal flows, weather conditions, participant abilities, and professional recommendations before selecting a destination. The duration and structure of a rafting adventure are equally important, particularly when coordinating participants with different ages, schedules, and endurance levels. In destinations such as Coloma and Lotus along California’s American River, groups can find opportunities for shorter outings, while rivers such as the Rogue and Salmon are also known for extended wilderness expeditions. Half-day trips offer a convenient introduction to whitewater, whereas full-day excursions provide more time for navigating rapids, enjoying scenic surroundings, and sharing experiences on the water. Multi-day adventures combine river travel with overnight camping, making them appealing to groups interested in a more immersive outdoor experience. Families with younger participants may prioritize accessible river sections and flexible itineraries, while corporate teams, reunions, and larger gatherings often place greater emphasis on group coordination and shared activities. Understanding these differences helps organizers select an experience that accommodates everyone’s expectations without compromising safety or enjoyment. Professional rafting outfitters can help translate these considerations into practical trip arrangements, particularly in established rafting destinations across California, Oregon, and Idaho. Companies such as Tributary Whitewater Tours , which has operated since 1978, provide guided adventures designed for different group sizes, experience levels, and occasions. Travelers organizing reunions, celebrations, or corporate outings can explore group rafting trips, while those planning adventures with children and relatives may find family rafting specials useful when comparing available options. These experiences demonstrate how trip planning can account for different participant needs, from choosing suitable rapids to coordinating equipment and logistics. Regardless of the destination or operator, reviewing age requirements, river conditions, trip inclusions, and safety procedures remains an essential part of organizing a successful group adventure. Turning Family Reunions Into Meaningful Outdoor Experiences Family reunions present a particular planning challenge because they bring together relatives whose ages, abilities, and interests may differ considerably. Traditional gatherings often revolve around meals, formal activities, and familiar conversations, which can leave younger participants restless and older relatives disconnected from the broader event. A thoughtfully selected rafting adventure introduces a shared activity that encourages family members to interact outside their usual roles and routines. Parents, children, cousins, and grandparents can participate in the same broader outing, even when some choose gentler rafting sections or alternative activities . This flexibility allows the reunion to center on a common experience without requiring every relative to undertake an identical level of physical challenge. The cooperative nature of rafting can be particularly valuable for families whose members live in different cities or rarely spend extended time together. In a raft, ordinary social divisions often become less important as participants focus on paddling, listening to instructions, and helping one another navigate the river. Younger relatives may gain confidence by contributing to the group’s efforts, while adults have opportunities to demonstrate encouragement and trust. Moments of laughter, unexpected splashes, and collective excitement can create natural conversation long after the river trip has ended. These experiences often feel more personal than heavily scheduled reunion activities because the strongest memories emerge from events shared rather than performances or entertainment arranged for an audience. Successful multigenerational rafting trips nevertheless require realistic planning and an inclusive approach. Organizers should ask about age limits, swimming requirements, physical demands, accessibility, medical considerations, and the availability of appropriate personal flotation devices before selecting a river. Some relatives may prefer to participate in nearby nature walks, scenic excursions, or group meals rather than enter the water, and those alternatives should be treated as part of the celebration rather than an afterthought. Scheduling sufficient breaks, providing comfortable accommodations, and allowing time for informal gatherings can help reduce fatigue and prevent an ambitious itinerary from becoming stressful. When families balance adventure with flexibility, rafting can provide an engaging centerpiece for a reunion while still accommodating the diverse needs of the people attending. Expanding Group Getaways Beyond Family Gatherings Although family reunions are a natural setting for whitewater rafting, the activity also lends itself to trips organized around friendship, professional relationships, and personal milestones. Groups of friends may choose a river excursion to celebrate a birthday, mark a graduation, or reconnect after years of living in different locations. Wedding parties and anniversary groups can incorporate rafting into a weekend itinerary that combines outdoor activities with dining and relaxation. Recreational clubs, university groups, and community organizations may use guided trips to introduce members to new environments and encourage participation in a collective challenge. What connects these occasions is the desire to replace passive entertainment with an experience that requires people to engage directly with one another. Corporate groups have additional reasons to consider rafting as part of a retreat or team-building program. Effective coordination on the water depends on clear instructions, attentive listening, adaptability, and the willingness to work toward an immediate common goal. These behaviors have parallels in professional environments, where teams must respond to changing circumstances while maintaining communication and trust. A rafting trip cannot substitute for structured leadership development, but it can provide a memorable setting for observing how colleagues collaborate outside their usual workplace responsibilities. When followed by thoughtful discussion, the experience can prompt useful conversations about communication styles, decision-making, and the importance of supporting colleagues under pressure. Planning a successful group getaway also means recognizing that excitement is not everyone’s primary motivation. Some participants may look forward to energetic rapids, while others may be drawn to the natural scenery, social interaction, or opportunity to try an unfamiliar activity. Offering a suitable river section and communicating the expected physical requirements in advance can help prevent less experienced travelers from feeling pressured to participate beyond their comfort level. For larger groups, organizers may consider dividing participants into smaller rafting teams while arranging common meeting points, meals, and evening activities. This approach allows people to enjoy experiences suited to their preferences while preserving the social benefits of traveling as one group. Planning the Logistics of a Successful Rafting Getaway The organizational details of a rafting trip can have as much influence on the overall experience as the river itself. Group organizers must coordinate participant numbers, transportation, arrival times, accommodations, meals, and the availability of guided departures. Popular rafting destinations can experience considerable demand during favorable weather and peak vacation periods, making advance reservations especially important for larger parties. Early planning also gives participants time to understand the itinerary, prepare suitable clothing, and disclose relevant concerns privately to the outfitter. A clear schedule with designated responsibilities can reduce confusion on the day of the excursion and leave more time for enjoying the adventure. Transportation and lodging deserve particular attention when participants are arriving from several locations. Some rafting operations involve shuttle transportation between launch and takeout points, while others require guests to meet at a designated base or staging area. Organizers should establish whether transportation is included, where vehicles can be parked, and how long participants should expect to remain away from their accommodations. For overnight getaways, lodging options may range from conventional hotels and rental cabins to organized campgrounds or outfitter-supported wilderness camping. Choosing accommodations near the rafting departure point can reduce travel complications, although the broader itinerary should also account for restaurants, grocery supplies, and opportunities for nonrafting recreation. Communication is particularly important when a group contains travelers with different expectations and levels of outdoor experience. A central planning document can summarize reservation details, payment deadlines, meeting locations, packing recommendations, emergency contacts, and contingency arrangements. Organizers should explain which expenses are covered collectively and which remain individual responsibilities, especially when optional activities or different lodging preferences are involved. It is also sensible to designate a primary contact who can communicate directly with the rafting company while ensuring that important updates reach the entire group. By resolving these practical matters before departure, organizers can prevent minor misunderstandings from overshadowing what should be a relaxed and rewarding occasion. Understanding Safety, Preparation, and Professional River Guidance Whitewater rafting takes place in dynamic natural environments, and even relatively gentle rivers require participants to take safety seriously. Water levels, temperature, currents, submerged obstacles, and weather can change the difficulty of a route, sometimes within a short period. Professional guides play an important role in assessing these conditions, selecting appropriate lines through rapids, and explaining how passengers should respond to common situations on the water. Reputable outfitters typically provide properly fitted personal flotation devices, helmets where required, and a safety briefing covering paddling techniques and emergency procedures. Participants should follow these instructions carefully and understand that guided rafting reduces certain risks without eliminating the possibility of injury or an unexpected incident. Preparation begins before participants reach the launch site, particularly for first-time rafters who may not know what to bring. Quick-drying clothing, secure footwear, sun protection, and suitable insulating layers can make a substantial difference in comfort throughout the trip. Cotton clothing may be unsuitable in cold conditions because it retains moisture and can contribute to heat loss, while specialized wetsuits or other protective equipment may be recommended depending on the river and season. Travelers should also ask whether medications, drinking water, and essential personal items can be carried safely in waterproof storage. Following an outfitter’s packing guidance is generally preferable to relying on assumptions about what a typical summer outdoor excursion requires. Physical readiness and honest communication are equally important components of a responsible rafting experience. Participants should inform the outfitter about relevant medical conditions, mobility limitations, pregnancy, or other circumstances that could affect their ability to participate safely. Age and weight restrictions may vary by river section, water conditions, and operator, so organizers should never assume that a trip suitable for one family or group will automatically be appropriate for another. Anyone uncomfortable with the anticipated level of difficulty should be encouraged to discuss alternative routes or activities rather than feeling obligated to join. A successful rafting outing is not measured by whether everyone attempts the most challenging rapids, but by whether participants can enjoy the experience within reasonable limits of safety and personal capability. Managing Costs, Seasonal Conditions, and the Value of the Experience Budgeting for a group rafting vacation requires a broader perspective than simply comparing the advertised prices of individual trips. The total cost may include guide services, equipment rental, transportation, lodging, meals, park or access fees, optional photographs, and gratuities. Multi-day expeditions often involve additional logistical arrangements, although some operators include camping equipment or meals within their packages. Larger groups may be eligible for specialized rates or private-trip arrangements, but pricing structures and minimum participation requirements differ among providers. Requesting a detailed written breakdown of included services can help organizers compare options accurately and avoid unexpected expenses after reservations have been made. Seasonality can affect both the cost and the character of a rafting adventure. In many Western U.S. river systems, spring snowmelt contributes to higher flows, while summer conditions may create opportunities for different types of trips depending on the watershed and water management practices. Dam-controlled rivers can offer more predictable release schedules on certain stretches, but release patterns and actual conditions still require confirmation. Water temperature, weather, environmental restrictions, and seasonal access may also influence the suitability of particular routes for beginners or younger participants. Organizers should evaluate these factors alongside school holidays, workplace schedules, and accommodation availability rather than selecting dates based on convenience alone. The value of a rafting trip is best assessed through the quality of the overall experience rather than the lowest possible price. A professionally organized excursion can eliminate much of the complexity associated with equipment, navigation, river access, and transportation logistics. For groups with limited vacation time, that convenience may be particularly valuable because it allows participants to concentrate on the experience instead of managing operational details. However, premium pricing alone does not guarantee an appropriate trip, making it important to review guide qualifications, safety procedures, cancellation policies, and the suitability of the selected route. A carefully chosen adventure can offer a strong balance of recreation, convenience, and meaningful group interaction without requiring an extravagant travel budget. Creating Lasting Memories While Respecting the Rivers The most memorable rafting adventures frequently involve experiences that participants did not anticipate when they first made their reservations. A challenging stretch of water may become a favorite story, while a peaceful section of river may provide the setting for an unusually meaningful conversation. Shared meals, photographs, wildlife sightings, and quiet moments at a campsite can become just as significant as the rapids themselves. For families, these memories may be retold at future gatherings, gradually becoming part of a shared history that connects different generations. For friends and colleagues, the experience can serve as a reference point for relationships that continue long after the trip has ended. Preserving the natural environment is essential to ensuring that future groups can enjoy the same opportunities for exploration. River ecosystems support fish, birds, vegetation, and other wildlife, while surrounding landscapes may contain sensitive habitats vulnerable to heavy recreational use. Participants should follow Leave No Trace principles, dispose of waste properly, respect wildlife, and comply with local regulations governing camping and river access. Responsible outfitters can support these efforts by educating visitors about local environmental conditions and encouraging practices that minimize unnecessary disturbance. For groups interested in more sustainable travel, considering an operator’s environmental policies and approach to resource stewardship can be an important part of the selection process. Whitewater rafting ultimately offers something that many conventional group vacations struggle to deliver: an experience in which participation matters more than observation. The setting encourages people to collaborate, adapt, and appreciate their surroundings while creating opportunities for spontaneous enjoyment and genuine interaction. Whether the occasion is a large family reunion, a weekend among friends, a corporate retreat, or a milestone celebration, the right rafting adventure can accommodate a range of goals and interests. Thoughtful planning, appropriate river selection, professional guidance, and respect for individual comfort levels remain the foundations of a successful outing. When those elements come together, a day or several days on the river can become far more than a recreational excursion, leaving participants with shared accomplishments and stories that endure well beyond the journey home. The post From Family Reunions to Group Getaways: Exploring Sustainable Whitewater Rafting Adventures appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: FDA Set to Approve First CRISPR Therapy That Edits Genes Inside the Body
items.description: Η εφάπαξ θεραπεία, lonvo-z, στοχεύει σε μια γενετική διαταραχή που προκαλεί επώδυνο και δυνητικά επικίνδυνο οίδημα στο λαιμό και σε άλλα σημεία του σώματος. Η γονιδιακή επεξεργασία θα μπορούσε να θεραπεύσει μια σειρά από θανατηφόρες κληρονομικές ασθένειες, αλλά οι τρέχουσες προσεγγίσεις είναι αργές, δαπανηρές και εξαντλητικές για τους ασθενείς. Μια νέα θεραπεία «ένα και τελειωμένο» που επεξεργάζεται τα γονίδια απευθείας μέσα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The one-time treatment, lonvo-z, targets a genetic disorder that triggers painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and elsewhere in the body. Gene editing could cure a host of deadly hereditary diseases, but current approaches are slow, costly, and grueling for patients. A new “one-and-done” therapy that edits genes directly inside the body could change the arithmetic and is on the cusp of approval in the US. Today’s only approved CRISPR treatment, Casgevy, works by extracting a patient’s blood stem cells, sending them away to be edited, and then infusing them back into the body. Each dose has to be made individually, and patients must first go through harsh chemotherapy to make way for the modified cells. Editing cells outside the body has been the established route so far because it sidesteps concerns about off-target edits and the difficulty of delivering the editing machinery to the right place in the body. It also means each treatment is bespoke, dramatically increasing the cost and complications. More recently, researchers have focused on approaches that edit cells inside the body . And now, Intellia Therapeutics has asked the FDA to approve a therapy that edits genes in the liver to treat a rare swelling disorder. The submission is based on promising results that show the treatment worked in patients for four years, according to Nature . The therapy targets a form of hereditary angioedema, a genetic disorder that triggers painful and potentially dangerous bouts of swelling in the throat and elsewhere in the body. Existing drugs can help prevent attacks, but they are only partially effective, access is patchy, and patients have to take them for life. Intellia’s new drug lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z) uses CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to switch off the gene that produces prekallikrein, a liver protein that causes blood vessels to leak fluid, leading to swelling in surrounding tissue. But rather than editing cells extracted from the body, the treatment encapsulates mRNA sequences encoding the CRISPR machinery inside tiny fat-based particles. After they’re infused into the blood, these nanoparticles travel to the liver, where prekallikrein is made, and are absorbed by liver cells. Once inside they release their cargo, and each cell reads the mRNA and builds the gene editing machinery itself. The newly constructed gene editor then cuts the cell’s DNA at the target gene, deactivating it. The infusion takes only four hours, so the whole procedure is done in a day. Clinical results so far have been encouraging. In an 80-person trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine in June, 62 percent of those given lonvo-z had no swelling attacks in the six months after treatment, compared with 11 percent of those who received a placebo. The treatment cut attack rates 87 percent overall and moderate or severe attacks 91 percent. The newly released long-term figures pooled participants from several trials, who had averaged more than three attacks a month before treatment. The number of attacks fell to fewer than 0.5 a month afterwards and stayed there for four years, with no serious safety events. “It’s very reassuring,” Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary-angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial, told Nature , referring to the four-year results. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.” For patients, Bernstein said, a one-off gene edit could replace a lifetime of managing medications to prevent and treat attacks. And it would avoid many of the hurdles that come with editing cells outside the body. But editing genes inside the body brings a different set of risks. For a start, there is no opportunity to screen out cells in which the CRISPR system has made unwanted edits elsewhere in the genome. Patients could also suffer harmful immune reactions to the treatment. Intellia already had one serious safety scare last year. The FDA put two of the company’s in vivo trials for a different disorder on hold after a participant with other health conditions died following treatment. The episode worries Sandra Christiansen, a hereditary-angioedema researcher and retired clinician at the University of California, San Diego, who told Nature she is uneasy about the unintended consequences of permanently removing a protein the body normally makes. “The question is really: Well, you are doing a permanent intervention, and you’re taking out a normal gene,” she said. “Could that be a problem?” Intellia is not the only group trying to edit genes inside the body though. Eli Lilly is testing a one-shot treatment called VERVE-102 that switches off a cholesterol-related gene in the liver using base editing, a more precise version of CRISPR. And Prime Medicine recently treated the first person in a trial using prime editing to fix a mutation behind Wilson disease , which causes copper to build up in the liver. If the FDA gives the go-ahead, lonvo-z would claim the title of the world’s first CRISPR medicine delivered directly into the body. Whether it lives up to its one-and-done billing, however, will depend on how patients fare in the years that follow. items.description: Διαφορετικές οδοί για τις καθαρές μηδενικές εκπομπές αερίων του θερμοκηπίου θα μπορούσαν να έχουν εξαιρετικά διαφορετικές επιπτώσεις σε άλλα μέρη του φυσικού περιβάλλοντος, σύμφωνα με μια νέα μελέτη. «Το πώς θα απελευθερώνουμε τις ανθρακούχες εκπομπές μπορεί να έχει εξίσου σημασία με το πόσο φιλόδοξοι είναι οι κλιματικοί μας στόχοι», λέει το μέλος της ομάδας μελέτης Alvaro Hahn Menacho, υποψήφιος διδάκτορας στο Ινστιτούτο Paul Scherrer (PSI) στο Zur.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Different pathways to net zero greenhouse gas emissions could have wildly different effects on other parts of the natural environment, according to a new study. “How we decarbonize may matter just as much as how ambitious our climate goals are,” says study team member Alvaro Hahn Menacho , a PhD candidate at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Zurich, Switzerland. Until now, most research on net-zero pathways has focused on cost and greenhouse gas emissions. Some studies have looked at the broader environmental context at a national level, but never at a global scale. The new work provides an opportunity to get a clearer picture of the tradeoffs involved before decarbonization infrastructure is locked into place, Hahn Menacho and his colleagues say. The researchers analyzed 24 different climate change mitigation pathways from three existing large-scale modeling efforts. The pathways involve a range of socioeconomic development patterns (for example, will population growth be high, or more modest?), climate ambition ( will the world decarbonize fast, or slowly? ), and energy system specifics (will the green transition involve a lot of wind and solar power, or a lot of bioenergy with carbon capture?). They assessed these scenarios with a life cycle analysis using a new open-source software tool, also developed at PSI, that enabled them to compare the future impact of the pathways on human health, to anywhere between a 13% decrease and a 354% increase in land use by the energy system, the researchers found. That’s because this figure strongly depends on the use of biomass. Pathways that rely heavily on bioenergy will require a lot more land to grow biofuel crops. Similarly, a pathway that relies more on carbon capture to soak up ongoing emissions will require a larger energy system and impose higher burdens on various aspects of the environment than one that prioritizes preventing emissions in the first place – even if the result is a similar emissions balance overall. “One particularly interesting finding was that ambitious climate goals primarily accelerate the demand for critical minerals rather than substantially increasing their cumulative extraction over the century,” Hahn Menacho says. Critical minerals are substances like lithium, cobalt, and nickel that are needed for green technologies but involve supply chain risks due to their scarcity or limited distribution. The finding “suggests that delaying decarbonization does not necessarily solve the resource challenge,” he says. The researchers aim to take these global insights and drill back down “to develop more geographically detailed impact assessments,” Hahn Menacho says. Among other research priorities, “an important next step is better understanding where these environmental pressures occur and how they can be mitigated.” Source: Hahn Menacho A. J. et al. “ Environmental and material implications of global climate mitigation pathways .” Nature Energy 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

items.descriptionOriginal: In a pocket park wedged between busy Montreal roads, the sound of ocean waves now washes over a neighborhood that has long carried a quiet grief - the displacement of islanders who left the Magdalen Islands generations ago and never quite left them behind. Researchers and artists collaborated to pipe in field recordings of coastal life, not as decoration, but as a form of cultural memory made audible, transforming a space people once moved through into one they now seek out. "Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource," says McGill professor Catherine Guastavino, whose team helped design the installation - and the results bear that out, with one resident now visiting specifically for "the boost it gives me afterwards." What the project quietly demonstrates is that the antidote to what alienates us in urban life may sometimes be found not in silence, but in the right kind of listening. It turns out that belonging can be transmitted through frequency, and that a community's sense of home need not be lost just because the geography has changed.

items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Phil Starks , an associate professor of biology at Tufts University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . During four days on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, I saw an Olympic marmot , a species found nowhere else on Earth; four bumblebee species working the same lavender plant; three western hermit crab species new to me; and five orcas slicing through the dark water off Ediz Hook . Any one of them could have been the trip’s highlight. Yet the encounter I cannot stop talking about occurred at low tide at Tongue Point , when I heard a barnacle. While I had seen thousands of barnacles, I had never imagined I could hear one. It made a noise that sounded like: Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Pop. As a professor who teaches about animal behavior , I know that the distinction between encountering an animal and actually noticing what it is doing is one of the simplest ways into natural history . It requires no laboratory and, at first, no special expertise. Mostly it requires learning how to let something ordinary become interesting again. At Low Tide My habit in places like a rocky shore is to become still and let my vision soften. Instead of staring at one point, I allow movement anywhere in the visual field to pull my attention. At Tongue Point, I was thinking about the demands of life in the intertidal zone , the shore between high and low tide: temperature swings, desiccation, and the cost of remaining clamped shut in open air. Then I noticed the soundscape. At first, the clicking was just coastal noise. I attributed it to small shore crabs moving among the mussels, or hermit crab shells knocking against them. Then one sharp pop pulled my attention to a single acorn barnacle . Its tiny opening was slightly unsealed, and two small plates were moving against its deeply ridged shell. The movement appeared to coincide with another pop. Then another. The repetition gave me something to follow. You can train yourself to do this almost anywhere. Watch honeybees fly around and see what you notice. When I take students or my sons to watch honeybees , I tell them not to stare directly at the hive entrance. Instead, sit nearby, look toward the open sky, and relax your gaze. At first you see empty air. Then a bee crosses it. Then another. Within moments the emptiness becomes a busy airport of arrivals and departures. Nothing new has entered the scene. You have just changed what you are capable of noticing. A Web of Assumptions Observation has its own traps. Sometimes you can miss behavior because it blends into the background. Other times you see something perfectly but stop asking questions because somebody has already told you what it means. Orb-weaver spiders offer a good example . Some add conspicuous bands or patches of dense silk to their webs. These structures are called stabilimenta , a name inherited from the old idea that they stabilize or strengthen the web. But they don’t. Researchers later found evidence for several possible functions: attracting prey, deterring or confusing predators, protecting webs from larger animals, and, in some cases, helping with temperature regulation. Different functions may matter in different species, environments, or stages of life. Muhammad Mahdi Karim/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA This orb-weaver rests on the stabilimentum of its web. I first became interested in the debate over stabilimentum function because I was unconvinced that one explanation could account for all the evidence. I started out asking whether somebody was wrong. The better question turned out to be why researchers expected one universal answer in the first place. That remains one of my favorite lessons from animal behavior: A name can be useful, but it can also sneak in an explanation. Once you think you know what something is, you become less likely to watch what it actually does. Seeing Isn’t Knowing The opposite mistake is just as easy: seeing something interesting and immediately deciding you understand it. After I returned from the Olympic Peninsula, I emailed a retired marine invertebrate zoologist and described what I had seen and heard. His response was delighted and appropriately skeptical: “Doubt it. Take a short video next time.” Aleria Jensen/NOAA/NMFS/AKFSC via Flickr How would you confirm these barnacles made a sound? I saw an open barnacle move and heard a pop at the same time. That is an observation. I did not demonstrate that the barnacle produced the sound. A mussel bed contains crabs, moving shells, and a host of other possible sources. A close-up video with synchronized audio could test whether the same visible movement repeatedly coincided with each pop. Noticing something is the start of science. It does not let you skip the work that follows. Look Again For anyone who wants to become a better naturalist , a simple sequence helps: Notice something. Describe it carefully. Ask what else could explain it. Decide what evidence would distinguish among those possibilities. Try it somewhere familiar: a backyard, city park, pond edge, patch of flowers, or shoreline. Stay longer than feels necessary. Let the sights and sounds become background. Then look for repetition. One movement, then another like it. One sound that separates from the rest. An animal returning to the same place. And once something catches your attention, resist the urge to explain it too quickly. Watch again. You may discover something genuinely unusual. More likely, you will discover something ordinary that you had never actually seen before. I may not have witnessed rare behavior at Tongue Point or identified a rare species. But I stayed long enough to wonder what I was hearing. Maybe that was rare enough. RELATED: What Are the Mysterious Creatures Quacking Under the Sea? We’re a Step Closer to Finding Out

Το μπολ με τη σούπα που θα σε είχε χορτάσει τον Μάιο μόλις και μετά βίας κάνει ένα βαθούλωμα, και κάπου γύρω στις τέσσερις θα ανταλλάξεις σχεδόν τα πάντα με μια ζεστή φέτα κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Maybe you’ve noticed it creeping in over the last few weeks. You finish lunch, and an hour later you’re already drifting back toward the kitchen. The bowl of soup that would have filled you up in May barely makes a dent, and somewhere around four o’clock you’d trade almost anything for a warm slice of something with cinnamon on top. It’s easy to blame the pumpkin bread and cider doughnuts suddenly everywhere you look, and they’re certainly not helping. But if you’ve been feeling hungrier in the fall, there’s more going on than seasonal temptation. Your body is responding to shorter days, colder air, and some very old instincts, all at the same time. Registered dietitian Lyndsay Hall of JM Nutrition walked through what’s behind that bigger appetite, and the good news is that none of it means you’re doing anything wrong. Why you feel hungrier in the fall Old instincts that haven’t caught up For most of human history, the end of summer meant leaner months were coming. “For those living in colder climates, fall signifies the transition from summer to winter, when historically food access would have been limited in the coming months, so people would eat more and put on some extra weight intentionally to help them get through the cold winter season,” Hall said. Your grocery store stays stocked all year, of course, but your body doesn’t know that. Like animals building up reserves before hibernation, some of that seasonal pull toward eating more may be wiring we’ve carried with us for a very long time. Staying warm takes energy Cold weather asks more of you physically, too. “When we start to feel physically cold, our bodies will expend more energy trying to keep us warm (i.e., by shivering) and diverting more blood flow to organs to keep them up and running,” Hall said. More energy spent means your body sends stronger signals to refuel. Less sunlight, shifting moods Then there’s the light, or the lack of it. “Many people experience a drop in serotonin levels during the fall and winter months due to decreased sun exposure and the cold weather making it difficult to get outside as often as we might during the summer months,” Hall said. Lower serotonin can affect hunger and fullness cues, making cravings stronger and meals feel less satisfying. For some people, the darker months bring more than a mild case of the winter blues . If low mood, fatigue, or changes in appetite start to feel heavy or stick around, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor, since seasonal affective disorder is common and very treatable. Holidays on the horizon Fall also kicks off the stretch of the year when so many gatherings revolve around food. “Over time, we have created psychological associations between certain times of year and eating more or indulging. Thanksgiving, for example, occurs in the fall months and is often centered around eating that many look forward to,” Hall said. The same goes for Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa and New Year’s, when the dishes on the table tend to be rich, hearty and tied up with memories. Staying satisfied through fall and winter None of this calls for a diet or a calorie tracker. Hall’s approach is to lean on three things that help meals stick with you longer: protein, fiber, and healthy fats. “Protein and fiber help to keep us physically satiated for longer periods of time,” she said. Together with fats, they slow digestion, so a cozy meal keeps you going well into the afternoon. Fold protein into the comfort foods you love Hall suggests stirring Greek yogurt or cottage cheese, or a high-protein plant-based alternative, into muffin batter, pancakes, and quick breads. A splash of milk or a dairy-free version in your oatmeal or morning latte works the same way. Eggs, tofu, fish and poultry can round out casseroles and pasta bakes, too. Let vegetables and legumes do the heavy lifting Soups, stews and chilis are perfect for this. Skin-on potatoes, winter squash, eggplant, peppers, leafy greens and green beans add fiber without changing the spirit of a dish, and apples or pomegranate seeds bring a bright, seasonal crunch to salads. “Beans, chickpeas and lentils are great ways to add both protein and lots of fiber to soups, stews, chilis and stuffed vegetables,” Hall said. Give seasonal baking a fiber boost Seasonal treats can pull a little more weight, too. “Oat bran, chia, ground flaxseed, grated zucchini or carrot, and dried fruits can be easy sources of extra fiber for any baked good or hot cereals,” Hall said. So the next time your stomach rumbles an hour after lunch on a gray November afternoon, you can take it as your body doing what it’s long been built to do. Answer it with something warm and filling, save room for the dishes that only come around once a year, and let the season be one you enjoy at the table instead of second-guessing every bite. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . Το χάπι του Αλτσχάιμερ, αναπτύξτε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A once-daily tablet called AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31 percent over a year in people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not on any other Alzheimer’s medication, according to phase 3 results presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. The Alzheimer’s pill, developed by South Korean company AriBio, belongs to the same drug family as Viagra. Across the full trial population, which included patients already taking other Alzheimer’s drugs, the effect did not reach statistical significance. How the Alzheimer’s pill works A PDE5 inhibitor, not an amyloid drug AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitor. Drugs in this class relax blood vessels, which is how they work for erectile dysfunction, and for the brain the effect is increased blood flow. Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the mechanism likely goes beyond circulation. “This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory ,” she said. That sets it apart from the disease-modifying treatments that have come through late-stage trials in recent years, which target amyloid, the protein that builds up into plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s. Dr. Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK , called AR1001 “especially interesting” for that reason. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function ,” she said. A tablet instead of an infusion The format matters too. Existing disease-modifying options require infusions or injections, while AR1001 is swallowed once a day. Dr. Richard Oakley, associate director of research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said that difference “could make treatment simpler.” Phase 3 trial results in detail 13 countries, 604 key participants The phase 3 trial, known as Polaris-AD , enrolled patients with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including the UK. The headline result comes from the 604 participants who were taking no other Alzheimer’s drugs, a group in which the decline in memory and thinking slowed by nearly a third compared with placebo. “Over the year of the trial, this drug was able to effectively slow down people’s decline in memory and thinking by nearly a third, and the side-effects reported were mostly mild to moderate,” Oakley said. The subgroup question The catch is in the wider group. Among patients who were also taking existing medications for Alzheimer’s symptoms, AR1001 did not produce a statistically significant benefit, which means the trial missed significance across its full population. Scales acknowledged as much. “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group,” she said. Oakley said the reason for that gap needs further investigation. Next steps for a new Alzheimer’s treatment Regulators and further trials None of the experts treated the results as final. All called for additional trials, and the findings still need review by independent scientists and drug regulators before AR1001 could be prescribed. Oakley also warned against improvising with existing drugs. “AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra, but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease,” he said, adding that people should not take Viagra to try to treat the condition. A different route against dementia The stakes are large. Alzheimer’ s is the most common form of dementia, and dementia is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050, with no cure available. Scales described the results as “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments,” and Oakley said they were “an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms.” If larger studies confirm the effect and explain why it disappeared in patients on other medications, a daily tablet working through blood flow would give doctors a second line of attack alongside the amyloid drugs. items.descriptionOriginal: Data from 10,000 workers show sit-stand desks boost active work time by 43 minutes a day—or roughly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. Every workday is a negotiation between our bodies and our jobs. Sit too long, our backs and necks protest; stand too long, our feet might have something to say about it. Sit-stand desks, also known as height-adjustable desks or standing desks, promise a healthier way to work, giving employees the flexibility to alternate between sitting and standing throughout the day. Now, new research suggests these desks may be giving employees, and employers, another benefit beyond ergonomics and well-being: productivity. Drawing on data from more than 10,000 employees, researchers at Texas A&M University found that workers who used sit-stand desks averaged 43 additional minutes of active computer use each day compared with those using regular desks, a difference that could translate to nearly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. The study, published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics , was co-led by Texas A&M School of Public Health professor Mark Benden and US Army Public Health Command Region, West, Regional Ergonomist Tricia Salzar. The findings suggest that the physical workspace may be a powerful, often overlooked, influence on employee well-being, productivity, and even a company’s overall performance. When organizations look to boost performance and productivity, they turn to new technologies, training programs and management strategies. But another powerful influence may be hiding in plain sight: the physical workplace itself. “It’s what we call the ‘workplace effect,'” Benden says. “The direct impact that the physical work environment has on the behavior, health, psychological well-being, and even engagement and performance of employees.” Sit-stand desks are a striking example of the workplace effect. Rather than locking employees into a single position for hours at a time, they give workers the flexibility to sit, stand and move throughout the day, as tasks and energy levels shift. “It can have a profound effect,” Benden says. “Alternating between different working positions promotes better health outcomes by reducing physical strain and encouraging movement for those who might otherwise spend most of their workday sedentary.” But the benefits may extend beyond physical health. Benden and Salzar’s new research shows that sit-stand desks can also have a substantial impact on productivity. “It has a cumulative, positive effect for both employers and employees,” Benden says. For employees, height-adjustable desks could lead to sustained energy and longer stretches of focused work. For employers, the higher work productivity could translate into a nearly $9,000 return on investment per employee annually. “The implications are hard to ignore,” Benden says. “When we design workplaces around employees and their needs, better health, better performance and better organizational outcomes follow.” The takeaway? Investing in the physical workplace, like height-adjustable desks, isn’t just good for employee comfort and health; it could be good for business, too. To test whether sit-stand desks could influence work output and productivity, Benden and his colleagues stepped out of their labs and turned to the real world, using a resource few ergonomics studies can match. “We analyzed a huge dataset of more than 10,000 workers over a yearlong period, comparing the total computer use of traditional desk users and height-adjustable desk users,” Benden says. The records paired employee comfort surveys with a digital trail of workplace activity, tracking everything from keystrokes and words typed to mouse clicks and typing errors, all to paint a detailed picture of how employees interacted with their computers throughout the workday. “It was important that we collected subjective measurements, like employee survey responses of their comfort and objective measurements of computer activity through software, to analyze how people engaged with their work,” Benden says. The team found that workers with sit-stand desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time, compared with 2.95 hours among regular-desk employees—a gap of about 43 minutes a day. That might not sound like much, but over a year it adds up to roughly 171 additional hours, or more than four 40-hour workweeks. And those additional hours come with a practical price tag, too. Multiplying the 171 additional hours by a standardized hourly wage of about $52, the researchers estimate that sit-stand desks could generate nearly $9,000 in potential annual productivity value per employee. “Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” Benden says. The researchers also found that employees using sit-stand desks generally typed more words and logged more keystrokes than their counterparts at non-adjustable desks. “The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way,” Benden says. For Benden, the findings open the door to broader questions about the future of organizations, focusing on another force rapidly reshaping the modern workplace. “Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into daily work,” Benden says. “Just as we’ve studied how the physical environment affects human health and performance, we’re interested in understanding how emerging AI technologies could influence the physical workspace and outcomes of organizations.” From adjustable desks to emerging technologies, the underlying question remains the same: how can organizations design environments and systems to better support the people who use them? “The next breakthrough may not come from working harder, but from designing workspaces and systems that help people work smarter and more efficiently,” Benden says. The story told by the more than 10,000 employees is that the desk may be doing far more than just holding up your computer. For Benden, sit-stand desks represent more than an ergonomic innovation. They’re part of a lifelong passion to understand how workplaces can be designed to better support employee well-being and organizational success. “We spend a lot of time at work,” Benden says. “It’s my passion to make sure that workers feel supported in their workplace, built on informed and guided scientific evidence.” A former Army Reserve officer, engineer, healthcare professional, inventor and world-renowned researcher, Benden has spent decades studying the complex relationship between people and the environments in which they work. So, the next time you find yourself slumping in your chair at 3pm with an aching back, don’t just reach for another cup of coffee, because the verdict is in: show this study to your boss. Your back—and your company’s bottom line—will thank you. Source: Texas A&M University The post Sit-stand desks boost active work time by 43 minutes a day appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. “As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. “Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning, environment and health initiative at ISGlobal, a public health research institute based in Barcelona. “Many cities are now following their direction: It reduces air pollution, noise, and livability improves.” Over the course of the 20th century, the city came to be dominated by vehicles. By the late 1990s, an average of 80,000 cars drove through Pontevedra every day — astonishingly, according to the municipality, three times more than through Madrid and five times more than London. Many of these vehicles weren’t even heading for the city, but rather transiting to other destinations such as beach towns on the coast. Those that did stay would turn the city’s charming historic squares into parking lots. Pontevedra before it was redesigned for pedestrians. Credit: Council of Pontevedra This came at a cost. Pontevedra’s epoch of cars dirtied the air, led to the deaths of pedestrians and seized centuries-old public spaces from residents. “The city was loud, disagreeable, unlivable,” says Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra, from the desk of his city hall office. “All the roads were filled with cars. The city was like a huge, permanent traffic jam.” Fernández Lores, a doctor by trade, decided enough was enough. In 1999, he campaigned to reclaim Pontevedra’s streets. The population agreed and elected him. Yet the urban transformation was not overnight. It has been carried out gradually. Fernández Lores began with a major effort to keep unnecessary cars out of the historic city center, removing significant amounts of on-street parking and only allowing essential vehicles to enter. Within one month in office, he had pedestrianized 300,000 square meters of the city center. In other parts of the city, he narrowed roads and widened sidewalks, introduced 30 kilometer per hour speed limits citywide, down from 50 kilometers per hour, and began installing traffic-calming measures like raised pedestrian crosswalks as well as almost 300 speed bumps. To take one example, the central Benito Corbel Street once had four lanes of traffic. In 2000, that was reduced to two lanes with widened sidewalks and trees. By 2014, it became a single-track road with only service vehicles able to enter, and even then for a limited time. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The mayor, who passed a Traffic and Mobility Plan for Pontevedra in 2011 formalizing and defining his pedestrian-first approach, also developed infrastructure to make it easier to ditch cars. The city now has roughly 4,500 private underground parking spaces and about 3,500 free “park and ride” spaces, all within a short walking distance from the center. Traffic lights were replaced by roundabouts to facilitate the flow of the remaining vehicles. In some central areas, the speed limit was lowered to just 10 kilometers per hour. Trees, green spaces and street lighting were also added to improve livability. But despite its reputation, Pontevedra is not completely car-free — it allows certain vehicles on its streets within reason. “It’s not a city without cars,” says Fernández Lores. “But we only let the ones that really need to come here in.” Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra. Credit: Peter Yeung Residents can drive to garaged parking spots in the city. People with disabilities are free to drive in Pontevedra as long as they have a permit. And vehicles used for emergencies and public services such as garbage and water trucks and ambulances are permitted 24/7. Home deliveries, house moving and loading and unloading by businesses are allowed, but only during certain hours. And indeed, taxi drivers like Barbosa may enter certain zones if they have a client or booking. When necessary, police can issue fines of several hundred euros, ensuring these limits are respected. “I think it was very smart, the decisions they made,” says Mirian Calvo , a researcher and expert in urban design from Pontevedra. “And this philosophy, of mixed-traffic, prioritizing soft mobility, has been applied over 30 years, more or less.” The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Car trips in the city center have fallen by 97 percent, according to official municipal figures. The air is markedly cleaner, with CO2 emissions dropping by about 70 percent. And the streets are much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011, whereas between 1996 and 2006, 30 people died in traffic accidents. (Pontevedra has won European road safety awards in the process.) The streets of Pontevedra have gotten much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011. Credit: Pilar Picas / Shutterstock In fact, about 90 percent of all journeys in the city center are by foot, with road safety so high that 80 percent of kids aged 6 to 12 walk without their parents to school each morning. Many local business owners have signed up to be supervisors if the children need help for any reason. For all the talk of the climate and safety benefits that come with limiting vehicle traffic and designing pedestrian-first urban spaces, however, there has been a surprising further advantage: Pontevedra is thriving economically. While in the 1990s, retail activity was drifting towards the suburbs, the decision to prioritize a compact, walkable city with a high quality of life, has changed the picture drastically. The mayor, for his part, has rejected proposals to build malls on the urban periphery, protecting the pedestrian-oriented urban core. “We don’t want huge malls, we want small, independent businesses,” says Fernández Lores. Pontevedra is now the fastest-growing city in the region of Galicia and in recent years has attracted 15,000 new inhabitants, mostly young families from elsewhere in northwest Spain. It also generates more jobs per capita than any other city in the region. The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Credit: Peter Yeung “It’s a very convenient city now,” says Calvo. “It’s a very nice city to live in and people can see that.” Most locals are effusive in their praise. Esther Louzao, 68, says that her home near Plaza Pelegrina was once surrounded by cars, but not anymore. She has even stopped driving to work, instead opting to go by bus. But she keeps her car for beach days. “I like it a lot, it’s easier to walk,” says Louzao, fittingly waiting at a bus stop. Pacing down the street with a stroller, Anna, a 39-year-old with a toddler son who lives four kilometers out of town, agrees. “It’s better, much safer, it’s pleasant,” she explains. “Even if sometimes my journeys take a bit longer.” Yet not all residents are entirely convinced by the policy. Manuel, who has been living in Pontevedra for 40 years, believes the transformation has been overstated. He owns three cars: one for the city, one for going to the beach and a third for sport driving. “Yes, the city is a lot different to how it was before,” says Manuel. “But it’s not as perfect as it seems. Some of us still need cars.” In Spain, all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants are now required have a low emission zone, like this one in Santander. Credit: Scharfsinn / Shutterstock Calvo agrees, noting that Pontevedra’s public transit network is lacking, which means that elderly people suffer and that cars must be taken to the coastal beaches. A system like Rome’s fleet of electric minibuses in the historic center could be implemented, she says. And although the results of Pontevedra’s policy are hard to deny, Calvo, who is also a lecturer in participatory architecture, argues that the system could have been even more effective and popular if residents had been more involved in the process. In the 2000s, she says, there was significant opposition to the project, even if that has now disappeared due to the clearly positive impact. “I don’t think there has been serious public engagement,” she says. “There are more things that could be done to make it more participatory.” Nieuwenhuijsen, however, commends Pontevedra’s less confrontational approach, which presented the restriction of cars as about livability. “I think everyone would prefer places with less noise and less pollution,” he says. “It shouldn’t be about the war on cars, presented as punishing someone.” In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free. Credit: OlgaVysh / Shutterstock In any case, cities across the world are following in Pontevedra’s pioneering footsteps. In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free by removing on-street parking spaces and restricting access. Freiburg, Germany, has similarly transformed the district of Vauban into a car-free zone, banning on-street parking and introducing vehicle speed limits at walking pace on residential streets. And in 2022, the Spanish government approved a royal decree requiring all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants to have a low emission zone, and recommending the use of traffic-restricted areas like that of Pontevedra. Yet not every place can easily replicate Pontevedra’s success. Professor Nieuwenhuijsen admits the transformation of North American cities could be more challenging given their size and lack of density. “U.S. cities were built around the car,” he says. “You get a lot of sprawl. European cities are different, many were designed for walking and horse carriages.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Likewise, transforming larger cities will not be as easy. Redesigning urban areas could be slowed or halted by infrastructure such as underground piping, adds Nieuwenhuijsen, and the investment required could prove prohibitive. Barcelona’s Superblocks cost as little as €500,000 but as much as €10 million per unit in some cases. But Fernández Lores, who is planning to run for an eighth term in 2027, believes that bigger cities could begin shifting away from cars and towards pedestrians by focusing on districts rather than entire cities. A case in point: In 2023, Culdesac Tempe, Arizona, became the first purpose-built, entirely car-free residential neighborhood in the U.S. “Cities work without cars,” he says. “But each city must find its own way.” The post The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
